林图尔把身子往车厢壁上一摔，咕哝着咒骂。「成家！——我此刻的心境更像上绞架！」他喊道。

「林图尔！」

「别折磨我了，父亲。普天之下再没有比我更惨的人了。把一个清白女人的名字跟我拴在一起？求一个姑娘——？看在老天份上，饶了我——让我去吧！」

「这是什么意思？」林多雷斯勋爵喊道。「你疯了吗，林图尔？你这里来这一套慷慨激昂，我全然没有防备。」

年轻人不作答。他把头探出去，迎着夜气的奔流和柔和的黑暗——树影、远山、稀少的行人，在黑暗里都成了影子。他平生呆看着外部世界的种种景象，看它们是什么便当它们是什么，从不多想。

「河岸边的一朵樱草，
在他眼里只是一朵黄樱草。」

===Original===

There had been no images or similitudes in light or darkness; but now another world had opened around him. He had a secret with the silence﻿—the speechless, inanimate things about knew something of him which nobody else knew: and who could tell when they might find a voice and proclaim it to the world? He uncovered his head to the air which blew upon him and cooled his fever. The touch of that cool fresh wind seemed the only thing in earth or heaven in which there was any consolation. As for Lord Lindores, he sat back in his corner, more angry than concerned, and more contemptuous than either. A woman has perhaps some excuse for nerves; but that his son, upon whose plain understanding he could always rely, and whose common sense was always alive to the importance of substantial arguments, should thus relapse into tragedy like his sisters, was more than he could tolerate. He would not even contemplate the idea that there was any cause for it. Rintoul had always been well behaved. He was in no fear of any secrets that his son might have to reveal.

“Rintoul,” he said, after a pause, “if you have got into any scrape, you should know well enough that I am not the sort of man to take it tragically. I have no faith in making molehills into mountains. I don’t suppose you have done anything disgraceful. You must be off your head, I think. What is it? You have been out of sorts for some time past.”

These words came like beatings of a drum to Rintoul’s ears, as he leant out into the rushing and sweep of the night air. There was a composure in them which brought him to himself. Anything disgraceful meant cheating at cards, or shirking debts of honour, or cowardice. Practically, these were about the only things disgraceful that a young man could do. An “entanglement,” a heavy loss at cards or on the turf, any other minor vice, could be compounded for. Lord Lindores was not alarmed by the prospect of an explanation with his son. But that Rintoul should become melodramatic, and appeal to earth and heaven, was contemptible to his father. This cool and commonsense tone had its natural effect, Lord Lindores thought. Rintoul drew in his head, sat back in his corner, and was restored to himself.

“I have been out of sorts,” he said﻿—“I suppose that’s what it is. I see everything *en noir*. All this business﻿—seeing to things﻿—the black, the house shut up﻿—”

===Chinese===

从前无论明暗，他心里都没有过什么意象或譬喻；可如今另一个世界在他四围打开了。他跟沉默守着一个秘密——那些无言的、无生命的东西，知道他的一点什么，是旁人都不知道的：谁能说它们几时不会开口，把它宣告给世界？他向吹在身上、给他退烧的空气袒露了头。那阵清凉新鲜的风的抚触，仿佛是天地间唯一含着安慰的东西。至于林多雷斯勋爵，他缩回自己的角落里，恼多过关切，而轻蔑又多于恼。女人家闹神经，或许还有个说处；可他的儿子——他素来靠得住他明白的头脑，他的常识对实打实的道理一向反应灵敏——竟也这样滑进他姐妹那一路的悲情里，这他不能容忍。他甚至不肯想一想这里头能有什么缘故。林图尔向来行事端正。他不怕儿子会有什么见不得人的秘密要露。

「林图尔，」他停了片刻说，「你若是惹了什么麻烦，总该如何道，我不是那种把事情往悲剧上办的人。我不信把鼹鼠丘堆成大山有什么好处。我不想你干下了什么丢人的事。我看你是失了常。怎么回事？你这阵子一直不大对劲。」

这些话传到把头探在夜风里的林图尔耳中，像一阵阵鼓点。话里有一种镇定，把他唤回了自身。「丢人」云云，无非是牌桌上作弊、赖掉赌债、或是临阵怯懦。实际上，一个年轻人能干的丢人事，差不多也就这几样了。一段「孽缘」、牌桌上或赛马场上一笔大亏空、随便什么不要紧的小过失，都可以设法弥补。同儿子作一场解释，林多雷斯勋爵并不发怵。可林图尔竟摆出这副苦情戏的做派，呼唤天地，在他父亲看来就鄙劣了。这副冷静常识的腔调自然见了效——林多雷斯勋爵这样想。林图尔把头缩回来，坐回他的角落，恢复了他自己。

「我是不大对劲，」他说——「想来就是这么回事。我看什么都是*一团黑*。这桩桩件件——张罗事情——一片黑，宅子关着——」

===Original===

“Let me warn you, Rintoul; don’t cultivate your susceptibilities,” said his father. “What is black more than blue or any other colour? This sort of thing is all very well for a woman; but I know what it is. It’s stomach﻿—that is really at the bottom of all tragedy. You had better speak to the doctor. And now, thank heaven, this Tinto business is over; we can get back to the affairs of life.”

===Chinese===

「我提醒你一句，林图尔；别养成这副多愁多感的脾气，」他父亲说。「黑比起蓝、比起随便什么颜色又多什么？这一套，女人家玩玩还罢了；我可看得透。是胃——一切悲剧本是从胃上来的。你最好去跟大夫说说。如今，谢天谢地，廷托这桩事过去了；咱们可以回到人生的正务上来了。」

===Original===

The rest of the drive passed in complete silence. And all the time they were together, Rintoul said not a word to his father about John Erskine. His situation was altogether ignored between them. It was not that it was forgotten. If these two men could have opened Dunnottar jail﻿—nay, could they have swept John Erskine away into some happy island where he would have been too blessed to think anything more about them﻿—they would have done it﻿—the one with joyous alacrity, the other with satisfaction at least. This gloomy incident was over, and Lord Lindores had no desire to hear any more of it. It was just the end that anybody might have expected Torrance to come to. Why could not the officious blockheads of the countryside let the matter alone? But he did not feel that desire to help and right John Erskine which his warm adoption of the young man to his friendship would have warranted. For why? such an incident, however it ended, would certainly spoil young Erskine’s influence in the county. He would be of no more advantage to anyone. A quarrel was nothing; but to escape from the consequences of that quarrel, to let a man die at the foot of a precipice without sending help to him, that was a thing which all the countryside turned against. It was this that had roused so strong a feeling against John, and Lord Lindores made up his mind philosophically, that though Erskine would probably be cleared of all imputation of blood-guiltiness, yet, innocent or guilty, he would never get over it, and, consequently, would be of no further use in any public projects. At the same time, his own views had changed in respect to the means of carrying these projects out. Lord Millefleurs was a better instrument than country eminence. A seat gained was of course always an appreciable advantage. But it was not certain even that the seat could have been gained; and a son-in-law in hand is better than many boroughs in the bush. The Duke could not ignore Lord Lindores’s claims if Edith was a member of the family. This was far more important than anything that could concern John Erskine, though Lord Lindores would have been heartily thankful﻿—now that he was good for nothing but to excite foolish sympathies﻿—if he could have got John Erskine happily out of the way.

===Chinese===

余下的一路车行，完全在静默中过去。两人在一起的全程，林图尔对约翰·厄斯金只字未提。他的处境被这父子俩整个略过了。倒不是忘了。这两个人倘若能打开邓诺特监狱的大门——不，倘若他们能把约翰·厄斯金一下子送到什么极乐岛上，叫他快活得再也想不起他们——他们是肯干的——一个干得欢天喜地，一个至少也干得满意。这桩阴惨的事故已经过去，林多雷斯勋爵不愿再听人提起。托伦斯落得这个下场，本在人人意料之中。乡里那些好管闲事的蠢货，为什么就不能撒手呢？可他并没有那份想去帮扶、想为约翰·厄斯金主持公道的热望——本来，他把这年轻人热络地收为朋友，是当得起这份热望的。为什么呢？这样一桩事故，不管怎样收场，必定毁掉小厄斯金在县里的号召力。他对谁都不再有用了。一场口角算不得什么；可是逃避口角的后果，任一个人死在崖脚而不遣人去救，那是全乡上下一致反对的事。正是这一条，激起了那样强烈地反对约翰的情绪；林多雷斯勋爵达观地打定主意：厄斯金多半能洗清血债的干系，然而，无论清白与否，他永远翻不过这一页，因此，于任何公共图谋都不再有用。与此同时，他自己在推行这些图谋的手段上，看法也变了。米勒弗勒尔勋爵比乡里的名流是更好的工具。争来一个议席，固然始终是看得见的好处。可那议席当初也未必争得来；到手的一个女婿，胜过林子里十来个选区。伊迪丝既做了公爵府上的人，公爵就不能不理会林多雷斯勋爵的诉求。这比任何关涉约翰·厄斯金的事都紧要得多——虽说，如今这人对他的用处只剩激起一些愚蠢的同情了——倘若他能顺顺当当地把约翰·厄斯金打发开，林多雷斯勋爵本会衷心感激。

===Original===

Millefleurs had reached Lindores some time before: he had returned direct from the funeral along with Beaufort, who, much marvelling at himself, had stood among the crowd, and seen Carry’s husband laid in his grave. The sensation was too extraordinary to be communicated to anyone. It had seemed to him that the whole was a dream, himself a spectre of the past, watching bewildered, while the other, whom he had never seen, who was nothing but a coffin, was removed away and deposited among the unseen. He had not been bold enough to go into the house to see Carry, even from the midst of the crowd. Whether she was sorrowing for her husband, or feeling some such thrills of excitement as were in his own bosom at the thought that she was free, Beaufort could not tell; but when he found himself seated at table that evening with her father and brother, he could not but feel that his dream was going on, and that there was no telling in what new scene it might unfold fresh wonders. The four gentlemen dined alone, and they were not a lively party. After dinner they gathered about the fireplace, not making any move towards the forsaken drawing-room. “This is a sad sort of amusement to provide for you,” Lord Lindores said. “We hoped to have shown you the more cheerful side of Scotch life.”

“I have had a very good time: what you might call a lovely time,” said Millefleurs. Then he made a pause, and drawing closer, laid his plump finger on Lord Lindores’s arm. “I don’t want to make myself a nuisance now; but﻿—not to be troublesome﻿—if I am not likely soon to have an opportunity of addressing myself to Lady Edith, don’t you think I had better go away?”

“You may well be tired of us; a house of mourning,” said Lord Lindores, with a smile of benevolent meaning. “It was not for this you came into those wilds.”

“They are far from being wilds: I have enjoyed myself very much,” said little Millefleurs. “All has been new; and to see a new country, don’t you know, is always the height of my ambition. But such a thing might happen as that I wasn’t wanted. When a lady means to have anything to say to a fellow, I have always heard she lets him know. To say nothing is, perhaps, as good a way of saying no as any. It may be supposed to save a man’s feelings﻿—”

“Am I to understand that you have spoken to my daughter, Millefleurs?”

===Chinese===

米勒弗勒尔早些时已到了林多雷斯：他跟博福特（Beaufort）一起从葬礼直接回来——博福特对自己大为惊讶，竟也站在人群当中，眼看着卡丽的丈夫下葬。那滋味太奇异，无从对任何人说起。他只觉得整场是一个梦，自己是往昔的一缕幽魂，茫然地看着另一个他——他从未见过的人，如今只是一口棺木——被抬走，安放进看不见的人堆里。他不够胆量走进宅子去看卡丽，连从人堆当中也不肯。她是在为丈夫悲伤，还是正怀着他自己胸中这一类的颤动——想着她自由了——博福特说不上；可当晚他发现自己与她的父亲和兄弟同坐一桌进餐时，他不能不觉出他的梦还在做下去，不知它会展开怎样的新场景、变出怎样的新奇。四位绅士独自用饭，这一席并不热闹。饭后他们聚在炉边，谁也不想挪往那间遭弃置的客厅。「拿这样的消遣款待二位，实在抱歉，」林多雷斯勋爵说。「我们本想让您看看苏格兰生活中较快活的一面。」

「我过得很好：你们可以说是一段美妙时光，」米勒弗勒尔说。随后他顿了顿，凑近些，把一根胖手指搭上林多雷斯勋爵的胳膊。「我不想这会儿惹人嫌；可是——不讨人烦的话——倘若我不大可能很快有机会向伊迪丝小姐表白，您不觉得我还是走为好吗？」

「您怕是厌烦我们了；一座居丧的宅子，」林多雷斯勋爵说，带着一层宽厚的意味深长的笑。「您到这些荒僻地方来，原不为的这个。」

「这里远不是荒僻：我过得非常开心，」小小的米勒弗勒尔说。「样样都新鲜；看一个新地方，您知道，向来是我野心的极致。可这种事也可能有：人家不想要我。一位小姐倘若真有话要对一个青年说，我一向听说，她自会让他知道。什么都不说，也许正是说『不』的顶好的说法。可以当它保全一个男人的感情——」

「我是否可以理解为，你已经向我女儿表白过了，米勒弗勒尔？」

===Original===

“I have never had the chance, Lord Lindores. On the very evening, you will remember, when I hoped to have an explanation, this unfortunate accident happened. I am very sorry for the gentleman whom, in the best of circumstances, I can never now hope to call my brother-in-law; but the position is perhaps a little awkward. Lady Edith is acquainted with my aspirations, but I﻿—know nothing; don’t you know?” said the little Marquis. He had his hand upon his plump bosom, and raised himself a little on one foot as he spoke. “It makes a fellow feel rather small﻿—and, in my case, that isn’t wanted,” he added, cheerfully. Nothing less like a despairing lover could be imagined; but though he resembled a robin-redbreast, he was a man quite conscious of the dignities of his position, and not to be played with. A cold chill of alarm came over Lord Lindores.

“Edith will return tomorrow, or next day,” he said; “or if you choose to go to Tinto, her mother regards you so much as a friend and favourite, that she will receive you gladly, I am sure. Go, then﻿—”

“No,” said Millefleurs, shaking his head, “no, that would be too strong. I never saw the poor fellow but once or twice, and the last time I had the misfortune to disagree with him; no﻿—I can’t convey myself to his house to learn if I’m to be taken or not. It is a droll sort of experience. I feel rather like a bale of goods, don’t you know, on approval,” he said with a laugh. He took it with great good-humour; but it was possible that even Millefleurs’s good-humour might be exhausted.

“I undertake for it that you shall not have to wait much longer,” said Lord Lindores.

===Chinese===

「我一直没有得到机会，林多雷斯勋爵。您总记得，我满心指望有一番解释的那个傍晚，偏出了这件不幸的事故。我很为那位先生难过——哪怕事事顺遂，我也再不能指望称他内兄了；可这处境多少有点尴尬。伊迪丝小姐知道我的痴念，可我——一无所知；您明白吧？」小侯爵说。他一只手按着他那胖胸脯，说话时一只脚微微踮起。「这叫一个家伙自觉挺渺小——而我这一款，本就用不着再缩小，」他快活地补上一句。再没有比这更不像绝望情人的人了；可是他虽然像只红胸知更鸟，却是个对自己身份的尊严有十足自觉的人，轻耍不得。一阵寒噤掠过林多雷斯勋爵。

「伊迪丝明天或后天回来，」他说；「要不然，你若愿意去廷托，她母亲那样把你当朋友、当心尖，一定乐意接待你，我确信。去吧，那就——」

「不，」米勒弗勒尔摇着头说，「不，那样就太重了。那可怜人我统共见过一两回，最后一回还不幸同他拌过嘴；不——我不能把自己运到他家宅子里去，打听人家收不收我。这是顶滑稽的一种经历。我觉得自己颇像一包货物，您知道，包退包换试看的那种，」他笑着说。他拿这事一团和气；可就连米勒弗勒尔的好脾气，兴许也有用尽的时候。

「我担保，不用再等多久，」林多雷斯勋爵说。

## XXXVIII / 三十八
===Original===

Rintoul had bad nights, and could not sleep. He had been in such constant movement that day that he was fatigued, and had hoped for rest; but after tossing on his uneasy bed, he got up again, as for several nights past he had been in the habit of doing, and began to pace up and down his room. The house was all buried in repose and silence﻿—the woods rustling round, the river flowing, the silence outside tingling with the never altogether hushed movements of nature; but indoors nothing stirring﻿—all dark; nothing but the heavy breath of sleep within the thick old walls. The fire was dying out on the hearth; the candles, which he lighted hastily, did not half light the room, but rather cleared a little spot in the darkness, and left all else in gloom. A nervous tremor was upon the young man﻿—he to whom nerves had been all folly, who had scoffed at them as affectation or weakness; but he had no longer that command of himself of which he had once been proud. His mind strayed involuntarily into thoughts which he would fain have shut out. They dwelt upon one subject and one scene, which he had shut his mind to a hundred times, only to feel it the next moment once more absorbing every faculty. His shadow upon the window paced up and down, up and down. He could not keep quiet. He did not care to have the door of his room behind him, but kept it in sight as if he feared being taken at a disadvantage. What did he fear? he could not tell. Imagination had seized hold upon him﻿—he who had never known what imagination was. He could not rest for it. The quiet was full of noises. He heard the furniture creaking, as it does at night, the walls giving out strange echoes; and never having kept any vigil before, thought that these strange voices of the night had to do with himself, and in his soul trembled as if he had been surrounded by enemies or spies searching his inmost thoughts.

===Chinese===

林图尔夜夜难眠。他白天奔波了一整天，早已疲惫，本指望睡一觉歇歇；可在床上翻来覆去睡不着，索性又爬起来，像前几夜养成的那样，在屋里来回踱步。整座宅子都沉入了安息与寂静——四围树林飒飒，河水流淌，屋外的静里颤动着大自然永不全然平息的动静；屋内却纹丝不动——一片漆黑；只有厚厚的老墙里透出酣睡的沉重呼吸。炉床上的火渐渐熄了；他匆匆点起的蜡烛，照不亮半个房间，只在黑暗里照出小小一块亮处，其余一切都留在昏暗里。年轻人身上起着一种神经性的战栗——他，一向把神经当作十足的蠢话，讥之为矫情或孱弱；可他再没有从前引以自恃的那份自制了。他的心不由自主溜进那些他巴不得关在门外的念头里。那些念头只缠着一件事、一个场面，他一百次闭目不看，下一刻又觉出它把他的心神整个吞了去。他的影子映在窗上，走来走去，走来走去。他安静不下来。他不乐意背对着房门，眼睛总盯着它，仿佛怕被人趁隙下手。他怕什么？他说不上来。想象力攫住了他——这个从来不知道想象力为何物的人。他为这个不得安生。寂静里满是声响。他听见家具在夜里吱呀作响，墙壁发出古怪的回声；他从未熬过夜，便当这些夜的声音都是冲着他来的，心里直打颤，仿佛四面八方围满了敌人，或是探着他心底念头的密探。

===Original===

Thus he walked up and down the room, keeping his face to the door. Did he expect anyone, anything to come in? No, no; nothing of the kind. But it is certain that sometimes along the long passage he heard sounds as of a horse’s hoofs. He knew it was nonsense. It was the sound of the river, to which he was perfectly accustomed; but yet it sounded somehow like a horse’s hoofs. He never would have been surprised at any moment to see the door pushed open and something come in. He knew it was ridiculous, but still he could not help the feeling. And the silence of the house was a pain to him beyond telling. One of these nights one of the servants had been ill, and Rintoul was glad. The sense that someone was waking, moving about, was a relief. It seemed somehow to give him a sort of security﻿—to deliver him from himself. But while he thus felt the advantage of waking humanity near him, he was thankful beyond description that the society of the house was diminished﻿—that his mother and Edith were away. He knew that they must have found him out﻿—if not what was in his mind, at least that there was something on his mind. During the last twenty-four hours particularly they would have been worse spies than the trees and the winds. How could he have kept himself to himself in their presence, especially as they would have besieged him with questions, with incitements to do something. They would have assumed that they knew all about it in their ignorance. They! They were always assuming that they knew. There was a fierce momentary satisfaction in Rintoul’s mind to think how completely out they would be, how incapable of understanding the real state of the case. They thought they knew everything! But he felt that there was a possibility that he might have betrayed himself in the very pleasure he would have had in showing them that they knew nothing. And it was better, far better, that they should be out of the way.

===Chinese===

他就这样在屋里踱来踱去，脸始终朝着门。他盼着有什么人、什么东西进来吗？不，不；没那回事。可千真万确，有时沿着长廊他会听见一阵马蹄般的声响。他知道这是胡思乱想。那是河水的声音，他听惯了的；可它不知怎么就是像马蹄。无论哪一刻，门被推开、有什么东西进来，他都不会吃惊。他知道荒唐，可这感觉偏摆脱不掉。宅子的寂静对他是一种说不出的煎熬。这些夜里有一夜，一个仆人病了，林图尔反倒高兴。知道有个人醒着、走动着，是一种宽解。那仿佛给了他某种安全感——把他从他自己手里解救了出来。可他一面觉出近旁有人醒着的好处，一面又感激不尽宅子里人少了——母亲和伊迪丝都不在家。他知道她们必定看穿了他——就算看不透他心里是什么，至少看得出他心里有事。尤其是过去这二十四小时，她们比树木和风还更像探子。有她们在眼前，他怎么守得住自己？何况她们还要拿问题围攻他，擻掇他做这做那。她们会凭着无知，自以为什么都懂。她们！她们向来自以为什么都懂。想到她们会错到什么地步、多么不可能明白事情的真相，林图尔心里掠过一阵凶狠的快意。她们自以为无所不知！可他又觉出一种可能：光是那份让她们瞧瞧她们其实一无所知的痛快，就够让他露出马脚了。所以她们不在跟前，是好得多、好得多的事。

===Original===

He did not, however, yield to this fever of the mind without doing what he could manfully to subdue it. He made a great effort now to fix his mind upon what his father had said to him﻿—but the names of Millefleurs and Lady Reseda only swept confusedly through his brain like straws upon the surface of the stream. Sometimes he found himself repeating one of them vaguely, like a sort of idiotical chorus, while the real current of his thoughts ran on. Lady Reseda, Lady Reseda: what had she to do with it?﻿—or Millefleurs, Millefleurs!﻿—they were straws upon the surface, showing how rapidly the torrent ran, not anything he could catch hold of. There was one name, however, round which that dark current of his thoughts eddied and swirled as in a whirlpool﻿—the name of John Erskine. There could not be any doubt that *he* had something to do with it. He had thrust himself into a matter that did not concern him, and he was paid for his folly. It was not *his* place to stand up for Carry, to resent her husband’s rudeness﻿—what had he to do with it? He was an intrusive, officious fool, thrusting himself into other people’s business. If he brought himself into trouble by it, was that Rintoul’s fault? Was he bound to lay himself open to a great deal of annoyance and embarrassment in order to save John Erskine from the consequences of his own folly? This was the question that would not let him rest. Nothing Rintoul had been a party to had compromised John Erskine. It was all his own doing. Why did he, for his pleasure, take the Scaur road at all? Why did he stop and quarrel, seeing the other was excited? Why rush down in that silly way with his coat torn to make an exhibition of himself? All these things were folly﻿—folly beyond extenuation. He ought to have known better; and whatever followed, was it not his own fault?

===Chinese===

不过他并没有束手屈从这心火，也尽了一个男子汉的力气去压制它。这会儿他竭力把心思钉在父亲对他说的话上——可米勒弗勒和雷塞达小姐那两个名字，只在他脑子里乱纷纷掠过，像水面上的草茎。有时他发觉自己含含糊糊念叨着其中一个，像一段傻气的叠句，而思想的真正潜流兀自奔涌。雷塞达小姐，雷塞达小姐：她跟这事有什么相干？——还有米勒弗勒，米勒弗勒！——那都是浮在水面上的草茎，只显出激流奔得多么急，不是他抓得住的东西。然而有一个名字，他思绪的那股黑流绕着它打旋、回旋，像卷进漩涡——约翰·厄斯金的名字。毫无疑问，出事跟他有干系。是他自己硬挤进一件与他无干的事里，他的蠢行得了报偿。挺身维护卡丽、愤恨她丈夫的无礼——这本轮不到他，跟他有什么相干？他是个好事的、多管闲事的蠹货，硬往人家的事情里插一脚。他自己惹了麻烦，难道怪林图尔？难道他就有义务把自己送上前去，受一大堆烦恼和难堪，好替约翰·厄斯金挡掉他自己蠹行的后果？这个疑问闹得他不得安生。林图尔参与过的任何事情，都没有连累约翰·厄斯金。全是他自作自受。他为什么偏偏图痛快，走了断崖那条路？为什么见对方火头上还停下口角？为什么衣服撕破了还那样傻头傻脑地冲下来，当众出丑？这一切都是蠹——蠹得无可开脱。他本该更明白些；如今不管生出什么后果，不都怪他自己？

===Original===

Along with this, however, there were other thoughts that flashed at Rintoul, and would not let him carry on steadily to the conclusion he desired. There are some things that are permissible and some that are not permissible. A gentleman need not betray himself: it is not indispensable that he should take the world into his confidence, if any accident happens to him, and he gets himself into trouble; but he must not let another get into trouble for him﻿—that comes into the category of the “anything disgraceful” which Lord Lindores was assured his son had never been guilty of. No! he had never done anything disgraceful. How was he to escape it now? And then, looking back upon all the circumstances, Rintoul sadly perceived what a fool he had been not to put everything on a straightforward footing at once. He reflected that he could have given almost any account of the occurrence he pleased. There was nobody to contradict him: and all would have been over without complication, without any addition from the popular fancy. It seemed to him now, reflecting upon everything, all the details that had filled him with an unreflecting panic then, that nothing could have been easier than to explain the whole matter. But he had lost that good moment, and if he made the confession now, every false conception which he had feared would be realised. People would say, If this was all, why make any mystery about it? Why expose another to disgrace and suffering? Rintoul had not intelligence enough, though he had always plumed himself on his common sense, to thread his way among those conflicting reasonings. He grew sick as the harpies of recollection and thought rushed upon him from all quarters. He had no power to stand against them﻿—to silence her who cried, “Why did you not do this?”﻿—while he held at bay the other who swooped down upon him, screaming, “How could you do that?” When it grew more than he could bear he retreated to his bed, and flung himself exhausted upon it, throwing out his arms with the unconscious histrionic instinct of excitement, appealing to he knew not what. How could he do this thing? How could he leave it undone? Rintoul in his despair got up again and found an opiate which had been given him when he had toothache, long ago, in days when toothache was the worst torture he knew.

===Chinese===

然而与此一道，还有别的念头向林图尔闪击而来，不容他把思路顺顺当当推到他想要的结论上去。有些事可为，有些事不可为。一个绅士未必要自曝其事：倘若遭了意外、惹上麻烦，他并非非得把内情和盘托给世人；可他不能让另一个人替他担罪——那就落进了「任何有失体面之事」的范畴，而林多雷斯勋爵（Lord Lindores）得到的保证是，他儿子从没干过这类事。没有！他从没干过有失体面的事。如今他该怎么脱身？于是回望这一切情由，林图尔痛心地看出，自己当初没有立时把一切摆在明处，是何等愚蠢。他想，当初那件事，他几乎可以随自己的意思随便怎么讲。没有人能驳他：一切本可以了结得干干净净，不生枝节，也不给众人的想象添油加醋。如今回想一切——那些当时叫他未及细想便惊慌失措的细节——他只觉得，把整件事讲明白本是再容易不过的事。可他错过了那个好时机，此刻再去招认，他当初担心的每一种误想都要变成现实。人家会说，既然不过如此，何必遮遮掩掩？何必让另一个人蒙羞受苦？林图尔虽一向以见识通明自许，却没有那份心智在这些相互撕咬的道理间穿行。记忆和思想的鹰身女妖从四面八方扑向他，他只觉得一阵阵发晕。他无力抵挡——堵不住这一个喊「你当初为什么不那样做？」，又挡不住那一个扑下来尖叫「你怎么能那样做？」。熬到受不了时，他退回床上，精疲力竭地一躺，激动之中凭着无意识的做戏本能摊开双臂，向不知什么求告。这事他怎么做得出来？这事他怎么撂得下？绝望之中林图尔又爬起来，找出一剂安眠药水——那是很久以前牙疼时人家给他的，在那个牙疼就是他所知最厉害的酷刑的年代。

He swallowed it, scarcely taking the trouble to mark how much he was taking, though the moment after he took a panic, and got up and examined the bottle to assure himself that all was right. It was nearly daybreak by the time that this dose sent him to sleep﻿—and he scarcely knew he had been asleep, so harassing were his dreams, till he came to himself at last, to find that it was eleven o’clock in a dull forenoon, his shutters all open, and the dim light pouring in. The horrors of waking when the mind is possessed by great misery is a well-worn subject﻿—everybody knows what it is to have Care seated by his bedside, ready to pounce upon him when he opens his eyes; but Rintoul had scarcely escaped from that dark companion. She had been with him in his dreams: he felt her grip him now, with no surprise, if with a redoublement of pain.

他一口吞下，几乎懒得看看自己喝了多少；可紧接着就慌了，爬起来端详药瓶，确认没有出岔子，这才放心。这一剂送他入睡时，天已快亮——梦魇纠缠得他几乎不觉得自己睡着过，直到最后清醒过来，发现已是阴沉上午的十一点，百叶窗全敞开了，昏沉的光泻进屋来。心里压着大悲苦的人醒来时的恐怖，是个写滥了的话题——谁都知道「忧愁」坐在床边、只等你睁眼便扑上来是什么滋味；而林图尔几乎没能从那位黑色的伴侣身边逃开。她一路跟着他入了梦：此刻他觉出她又攫住了自己，并不惊讶，只是痛上加痛。

It was nearly midday when he got downstairs, and he found nobody. His father was out. Millefleurs was out. His breakfast was arranged upon a little table near the fire, his letters laid ready, the county newspaper﻿—a little innocent broadsheet﻿—by his plate. But he could not take advantage of any of these luxuries; he swept his letters into his pocket, flung the paper from him, then reflected that there might *be something in it*, and picked it up again with trembling hands. There was *something in it*. There was an account of the private examination before the sheriff of Mr. John Erskine of Dalrulzian on suspicion of being concerned in the death of the late lamented Mr. Torrance of Tinto. “From circumstances which transpired,” the sheriff, the newspaper regretted to say, had thought it right to relegate Mr. Erskine to Dunnottar jail, there to await the result of a more formal inquiry, to be held on the 25th at Dunearn. “We have little fear that a gentleman so respected will easily be able to clear himself,” it was added; and “a tribute of respect to the late Patrick Torrance﻿—a name which, for genial bonhomie and sterling qualities, will long be remembered in this county,” wound up the paragraph. The greater portion of its readers, already acquainted with the news by report, read it with exclamations of concern, or cynical rustic doubt whether John Erskine was so much respected, or Pat Torrance as sure of a place in the county’s memory, as the *Dunearn Sentinel* said; but all Rintoul’s blood seemed to rush to his head and roar like a torrent in his ears as he read the paragraph. He could hear nothing but that rushing of excitement and the bewildered half-maddened thoughts which seemed to accompany it. What was he to do? What was he to do?

他下楼时已近正午，一个人也没碰见。父亲出去了。米勒弗勒出去了。他的早餐摆在炉边一张小桌上，信件理好了放在一旁，郡报——一张清白无辜的小报——擱在盘子边。可这些享受他一样也消受不了；他把信一古脑儿扫进口袋，把报纸甩开，转念一想那里面兴许有文章，又双手发颤地捡了回来。里头果然有文章。有一篇报道，说达尔鲁尔齐恩的约翰·厄斯金先生，因涉嫌与已故托伦斯先生之死有牵连，在郡法官面前受了非公开审问。「根据透露出的种种情况」，报上说，郡法官深以为憾，认为理应将厄斯金先生移送邓诺塔监狱，听候将于二十五日在邓恩举行的更正式的调查。「我们毫不担心，这样一位深受敬重的绅士定能轻易洗清自身，」报道补了一句；又以「向已故帕特里克·托伦斯先生致哀——这个以其温厚风趣和真诚品质而长久留驻本郡记忆的名字」一段，收束了这段文字。读者中的大多数早已从传闻中得知消息，读时或惊叹忧虑，或带着乡野式的刻薄狐疑：约翰·厄斯金是否真那么受敬重，帕特·托伦斯是否真稳稳占得住郡人的记忆，未必像《邓恩哨卫报》说的那样；可林图尔读着这段文字，浑身的血仿佛都涌上头顶，在耳中轰鸣如山洪。除了那阵激动的奔涌和随之而来的昏乱半狂的念头，他什么也听不见了。他该怎么办？他该怎么办？

There was a little interval, during which Rintoul literally did not know what he was doing. His mind was not prepared for such an emergency. 有那么一小段时间，林图尔当真不知道自己在做什么。他的头脑全无应付这种变故的准备。他像一只软木塞，在自己思绪的沸流上翻滚——无助，惶惑，被冲来撞去。直到湿漉漉的空气扑上脸，他才发现自己已经徒步上了去邓恩的路：眼前是高高低低的屋顶线，市政厅的高塔直指阴沉的天空，从一片屋宇中突出来，像个路标，指明他该走的路。一望见那座塔，他猛然回过神来，立刻开始对行动恢复几分有意识的掌控。心里的运转清楚了些；惊慌平息了些。说到底，谁能害得了约翰·厄斯金？他是很傻；他让自己惹上了嫌疑；可毫无疑问，这样一位深受敬重的绅士定能洗清自己——这样一位深受敬重的绅士。林图尔一遍遍对自己念着这句话，就像前一夜念着米勒弗勒和雷塞达小姐的名字。对约翰·厄斯金来说，把自己的开释和清白的完全认定推到二十五号，又有什么要紧？倘若他害了重感冒，结果也一样——闭门不出，兴许还得困在卧房里。那算什么？什么都不算：一桩小小的不便，谁都可能摊上。而且毫无疑问，这样一位深受敬重的绅士——到时候自有证据还他清白：从来没有过的事，不可能拿出什么凭据来；必要时全郡的人都可以为约翰·厄斯金的品行作证——他不是好寻衅斗殴的人；他跟——他跟人家之间没有任何口角的缘由——

Rintoul’s feet, which had been going rapidly towards Dunearn, went on slower and slower. He came to a pause altogether about a mile from the town. Was it necessary to go any farther? What could he do today? Certainly there would be no advantage to Erskine in anything he did today. He turned round slowly, and went back towards Lindores. Walking that way, there was nothing but the long sweep of the landscape between him and Tinto, to which his eyes could not but turn as he walked slowly on. The flag was up again﻿—a spot of red against the dull sky﻿—and the house stood out upon its platform with that air of ostentation which fretted the souls of the surrounding gentry. Rintoul could not bear the sight of it: it smote him with a fierce impatience. Scarcely conscious that his movement of hot and hasty temper was absurd, he turned round again to escape it, and set his face towards the emblem of severe justice and the law, the tower of the Town House of Dunearn. When this second monitor made itself visible, a kind of dull despair took possession of him. His steps were hemmed in on every side, and there was no escape.

林图尔的双脚本来在快步赶往邓恩，越走越慢。离城约一英里，他索性站住了。还有必要再走吗？他今天能做什么？可以肯定，他今天做的任何事，都于厄斯金无益。他缓缓转过身，往林多雷斯走回去。这一路走去，他与廷托之间只隔着一道绵延的田野，他缓缓走着，眼睛不由自主往那边望。旗子又升起来了——阴沉天空底下一红斑——宅子立在台地上，一副招摇的神气，刺得四邻乡绅们心里发毛。林图尔看不得那景象：它激起他一阵凶暴的烦躁。他几乎没意识到自己这股火急性子有多可笑，又转过身去躲开它，把脸朝着严峻正义与法律的象征——邓恩市政厅的高塔。等这第二位监工也显现在眼前，一种沉沉的绝望把他攫住了。他的脚步四面受围，无处可逃。

It was while he was moving on thus reluctantly, by a sort of vague compulsion, that he recognised, with amazement, Nora Barrington coming towards him. It was a piece of good fortune to which he had no right. She was the only creature in the world whose society could have been welcome to him. They met as they might have met in a fairy tale: fairy tales are not over, so long as people do meet in this way on the commonplace road. They had neither of them thought of any such encounter﻿—he, because his mind was too dolorous and preoccupied for any such relief; she, because Rintoul seldom came into Dunearn, and never walked, so that no idea of his presence occurred to her. She was going to fulfil a commission of Miss Barbara’s, and anxious if possible to see Edith, which was far more likely than Edith’s brother. They were both surprised, almost beyond speech; they scarcely uttered any greeting. It did not seem strange, somehow, that Rintoul should turn and walk with her the way she was going, though it was not his way. And now a wonderful thing happened to Rintoul. His ferment of thought subsided all at once﻿—he seemed to have sailed into quiet seas after the excitement of the headlong current which had almost dashed him to pieces. He did not know what it meant. The storm ended, and there stole over him “a sound as of a hidden brook, in the leafy month of June.” And Nora felt a softening of sympathetic feeling, she did not know why. She was sorry for him. Why should she have been sorry for Lord Rintoul? He was infinitely better off than she was. She could not account for the feeling, but she felt it all the same. She asked him first how Lady Caroline was﻿—poor Lady Caroline!﻿—and then faltered a little, turning to her own affairs.

“I hope I shall see Edith before I go away. Do you know when they are coming back? I am going home﻿—very soon now,” Nora said. She felt almost apologetic﻿—reluctant to say it﻿—and yet it seemed necessary to say it. There were many people whom she might have met on the road to whom she would not have mentioned the fact, but it seemed incumbent upon her now.

“Going away! No, that you must not do﻿—you must not do it! Why should you go away?” he cried.

正这样半推半就、被一种说不清的力道驱赶着往前走时，他惊讶地认出，迎面走来的是诺拉·巴林顿（Nora Barrington）。这是一份他没有福分消受的好运。她是世上唯一一个他乐意作伴的人。他们这样相逢，就像童话里的相逢：只要人们还能这样在寻常的路上相遇，童话就没有过时。他们俩谁都没料到这场相遇——他，是因为心里愁苦重重，装不下这样的宽慰；她，是因为林图尔难得进邓恩，更从不步行，压根没想到他会在。她正要去替芭芭拉小姐办一件差事，还盼着能见上伊迪丝——那可比撞见伊迪丝的哥哥容易得多。两人都惊得几乎说不出话；问候的话都没大说出口。不知怎么，林图尔转身陪她顺着她的方向同走，虽然并不是他的路，却也不显得奇怪。这时，一桩奇妙的事降临到林图尔身上。他翻腾的思绪一下子平息了——方才那股几乎把他摔碎的激流狂潮过后，他仿佛驶入了平静的海。他不知道这是什么缘故。风暴止息了，一种「如同六月枝叶月份里一道隐秘溪流的声响」悄悄漫过他全身。而诺拉也觉出一阵同情的软意，她说不清为什么。她为他难过。她为什么要为林图尔勋爵难过？他的境况比她好出千百倍。这感觉无从解释，可她偏偏就是觉到了。她先问起卡罗琳夫人的情况——可怜的卡罗琳夫人！——随后迟疑了一下，转到了自己的事上。

「我盼着走之前能见伊迪丝一面。你知道他们什么时候回来吗？我要回家了——就这几天了。」诺拉说。她几乎觉得抱歉——不愿说出口——可又觉得非说不可。这一路上她可能遇见的许多人，她本不会提起这件事，可此刻却像担着义务似的非说不行。

「回家去！不，你可不能走——不能走！你为什么要走？」他喊道。

===Original===

“There are many reasons.” Nora felt that she ought to laugh at his vehemence, or that, perhaps, she should be angry; but she was neither the one nor the other﻿—only apologetic, and so sorry for him. “Of course I always knew I should have to go: though I shall always think it home here, yet it is not home any longer. It is a great pity, don’t you think, to live so long in a place which, after all, is not your home?”

“I cannot think it a great pity that you should have lived here,” he said. “The thing is, that you must not go. For God’s sake, Nora, do not go! I never thought of that; it is the last drop. If you knew how near I am to the end of my strength, you would not speak of such a thing to me.”

“Lord Rintoul! I﻿—don’t understand. What can it matter?” cried Nora, in her confusion. She felt that she should have taken a different tone. He had no right to call her Nora, or to speak as if he had anything to do with her coming or going. But the hurried tone of passion and terror in his voice overwhelmed her. It was as if he had heard of the last misfortune that could overwhelm a man.

“Matter! Do you mean to me? It may not matter to anyone else; to me it is everything,” he said, wildly. “I shall give in altogether. I shall not care what I do if you go away.”

“Now, Lord Rintoul,” said Nora, her heart beating, but trying to laugh as she best could, “this, you must know, is nonsense. You cannot mean to make fun of me, I am sure; but﻿—I don’t know what you mean. We had better say no more about it.” Then she melted again. She remembered their last interview, which had gone to her heart. “I know,” she said, “that you have been in a great deal of trouble.”

“You know,” said Rintoul, “because you feel for me. Nobody else knows. Then think what it will be for me if you go away﻿—the only creature whom I dare to speak to. Nora, you know very well I was always fond of you﻿—from the first﻿—as soon as we met﻿—”

“Don’t, don’t, Lord Rintoul! I cannot get away from you on this public road. Have some respect for me. You ought not to say such things, nor I to hear.”

===Chinese===

「缘由多着呢。」诺拉觉得，对这般激烈，她本该一笑置之，或者，也许该动气；可她两样都不是——只有歉意，还有满心的怜惜。「当然，我向来知道我总有一天得走：虽说我会永远把这里当家，可它终究不再是家了。在一个到底不是自己家的地方住了这么久，你说可惜不可惜？」

「你在这里住过，我可一点不觉得可惜，」他说。「要紧的是，你不能走。看在老天爷分上，诺拉，别走！我没想到这一层；这是压垮我的最后一滴。你要是知道我的力气已经用到头了，就不会对我说这种事。」

「林图尔勋爵！我——我不明白。这有什么要紧？」诺拉慌乱地喊道。她觉得本该换一副口气。他没有权利叫她诺拉，也没有权利摆出一副她的去留与他相干的样子。可他声音里那股又狂乱又惶恐的急切把她压倒了。那模样，仿佛他刚听见了能把一个人彻底压垮的最后一场祸事。

「要紧！你是说对我？对别人也许无所谓；对我是全部。」他狂乱地说。「你会叫我整个垮掉的。你若走了，我干什么都不在乎了。」

「好了，林图尔勋爵，」诺拉说，心在跳，却尽量笑一笑，「你该知道，这是胡话。我相信你不是存心拿我打趣；可是——我不明白你的意思。这话咱们还是别再说了。」随即她又软了下来。她想起他们上回的那次交谈，那曾深深刻在她心上。「我知道，」她说，「你遭了很多难。」

「你知道，是因为你体恤我。别人都不知道。那么想想，你若走了，对我算什么——你是唯一一个我敢说话的人。诺拉，你心里很明白，我一向喜欢你——从最初——从我们一见面——」

「别说了，别说了，林图尔勋爵！在这大路上我又躲不开你。你放尊重些。这种话你不该说，我也不该听。」

===Original===

He looked at her, wondering. “Is it any want of respect to tell you that you are the girl I have always wanted to marry? You may not feel the same; it may be only your kindness: you may refuse me, Nora; but I have always meant it. I have thought it was our duty to do the best we could for the girls, but I never gave in to that for myself. My father has spoken of this one and that one, but I have always been faithful to you. That is no want of respect, though it is a public road. From the time I first knew you, I have only thought of you.”

What an ease it gave him to say this! All the other points that had so occupied him before seemed to have melted away in her presence. If he had but someone to stand by him﻿—if he had but Nora, who felt for him always. It seemed that everything else would arrange itself, and become less difficult to bear.

As for Nora, she had known very well that Rintoul was, as he said, fond of her. It is so difficult to conceal that. But she thought he would “get over it.” She had said to herself, with some little scorn, that he never would have the courage to woo a poor girl like herself﻿—a girl without anything. He had a worldly mind though he was young, and Nora had never allowed herself to be deluded, she thought.

“Don’t you believe me?” he said, after a moment’s pause, looking at her wistfully, holding out his hand.

“Yes, I believe you, Lord Rintoul,” said Nora; but she took no notice of his outstretched hand, though it cost her something to be, as she said to herself, “so unkind.” “I do believe you; but it would never be permitted, you know. You yourself would not approve of it when you had time to think; for you are worldly-minded, Lord Rintoul: and you know you ought to marry﻿—an heiress﻿—someone with money.”

“You have a very good right to say so,” he replied. “I have always maintained that for the girls: but if you had ever taken any notice of me, you would have found out that I never allowed it for myself. Yes, it is quite true I am worldly-minded; but I never meant to marry money. I never thought of marrying anyone but you.”

===Chinese===

他望着她，一脸讶异。「告诉你，你正是我一直想娶的姑娘，这算哪门子不尊重？你可以没有同样的心思；那也许只是你心肠好：你可以拒绝我，诺拉；可我从来是认真的。我素来认为，替妹妹们谋最好的亲事是我们的本分，可我自己从不认这一条。我父亲提过这个、提过那个，我心里始终只有你。这算不得不尊重，虽然这是条大路。从我认识你起，我心里想的就只有你。」

说出这番话，对他是一种怎样的松快！先前死死缠着他的那一切，在她的面前仿佛都消融了。倘若有人与他并肩站着——倘若他有诺拉，那个永远体恤他的诺拉。其余的一切仿佛自会各归其位，变得不那么难捱。

至于诺拉，她早就十分清楚，林图尔正如他自己所说，喜欢她。这种事是藏不住的。可她想他总会「想开的」。她曾带着些许轻蔑对自己说，他永远鼓不起勇气来向她这样一无所有的穷姑娘求亲——一个什么都没有的姑娘。他虽然年轻，却一身世俗气，诺拉从不许自己受骗，她是这样想的。

「你不信我么？」顿了片刻，他若有所望地望着她，伸出手来。

「信，我信你，林图尔勋爵，」诺拉说；可她对那只伸出的手未予理会，尽管用她自己的话说，做一回「这样狠心的人」，也让她付出了些代价。「我是信你的；可这永远不会被允许的，你知道。等你冷静下来细想，你自己也不会赞成；因为你满脑子世俗，林图尔勋爵：你知道你该娶——娶一位女继承人——娶个有钱的。」

「你完全有权利这么说，」他答道。「替妹妹们，我一向也是这么主张的：可你要是平素肯理睬我一点，你就会发现，对我自己我从不认这一条。不错，我一身世俗气，这千真万确；可我从来没想娶钱财。除了你，我从没想过娶任何人。」

===Original===

And now there was a pause again. He did not seem to have asked her any question that Nora could answer. He had only made a statement to her that she was the only girl he had ever wished to marry. It roused a great commotion in her breast. She had always liked Rintoul, even when his sisters called him a Philistine; and now when he was in trouble, under some mysterious shadow, she knew not why, appealing to her sympathy as to his salvation, it was not possible that the girl should shut her heart against him. They walked on together for a few yards in silence, and then she said, faltering, “I had better go back now﻿—I﻿—did not expect to﻿—meet anyone.”

“Don’t go back without saying something to me. Promise me, Nora, that you will not go away. I want you! I want you! Without you I should go all wrong. If you saw me sinking in the water, wouldn’t you put out your hand to help me?﻿—and that is nothing to what may happen. Nora, have you the heart to go back without saying anything to me?” cried Rintoul, once more holding out his hand.

There was nobody visible on the road, up or down. The turrets of Lindores peeped over the trees in the distance, like spectators deeply interested, holding their breath; at the other end the long thin tower of the Town House seemed to pale away into the distance. He looked anxiously into her face, as if life and death hung on the decision. They had come to a standstill in the emotion of the moment, and stood facing each other, trembling with the same sentiment. Nora held back still, but there was an instinctive drawing closer of the two figures﻿—irresistible, involuntary.

“Your father will never consent,” she said, with an unsteady voice; “and my father will never allow it against his will. But, Lord Rintoul﻿—”

“Not lord, nor Rintoul,” he said.

“You never liked to be called Robin,” Nora said, with a half malicious glance into his face. But poor Rintoul was not in the humour for jest. He took her hand, her arm, and drew it through his.

“I cannot wait to think about our fathers. I have such need of you, Nora. I have something to tell you that I can tell to no one in the world but you. I want my other self to help me. I want my wife, to whom I can speak﻿—”

===Chinese===

接着又是一阵沉默。他似乎并没有问她什么诺拉能回答的问题。他只是向她宣告了一件事：她是他唯一想娶过的姑娘。这在她胸中搜起一片大乱。她一向喜欢林图尔，哪怕姐妹们骂他俗物的时候也喜欢；而如今他遭了难，罩在一重神秘的阴影下——她不知是何缘故——把她的怜恤当作救命稻草一般仰求着，姑娘的心也就无法对他关闭了。两人默默同走了几步，随后她迟疑着说：「我现在还是回去吧——我——没想着——会遇上人。」

「别什么都不说就回去。答应我，诺拉，答应我你不走。我需要你！我需要你！没有你，我就全完了。你要是看见我在水里往下沉，能不伸手拉我吗？——而可能落到我头上的事，比那还重得多。诺拉，你忍心什么话都不留就回去吗？」林图尔喊道，又一次伸出手来。

大路上下，一个人影也望不见。林多雷斯的角楼从远处的树梢上探出来，像屏住呼吸、看得出神的看客；另一头，市政厅细长的高塔仿佛淡淡消隐进远方。他焦灼地盯着她的脸，仿佛生死悬在这一决。两人在这一刻的激动里停住了脚，面对面站着，因同一种情绪而战栗。诺拉还在退让，可两个身影之间有一股本能的靠近——不可抗拒，不由自主。

「你父亲永远不会答应，」她声音发颤地说；「我父亲也永远不肯违背他的意思。可是，林图尔勋爵——」

「别叫勋爵，也别叫林图尔。」他说。

「可你从来不乐意人家叫你罗宾呀。」诺拉说着，半带狡黢地瞥了他一眼。可可怜的林图尔没有打趣的心思。他握住她的手、她的臂，把它挽进自己臂弯里。

「等不及去想咱们的父亲了。我这样需要你，诺拉。我有一件事要对你说，这世上除了你，我对谁都说不出。我要我另一个自己来帮我。我要我的妻子，一个我能够说话的人——」

===Original===

His arm was quivering with anxiety and emotion. Though Nora was bewildered, she did not hesitate﻿—what girl would?﻿—from the responsibility thus thrust upon her. To be so urgently wanted is the strongest claim that can be put forth upon any human creature. Instinctively she gave his arm a little pressure, supporting rather than supported, and said “Tell me,” turning upon him freely, without blush or faltering, the grave sweet face of sustaining love.

===Chinese===

他的手臂因焦灼和激动而微微发颤。诺拉虽然心乱，却并没有畏缩——哪个姑娘会畏缩呢？——面对这样落到她肩上的责任。被人这样急切地需要，是一个人能对另一个人提出的最强有力的要求。她本能地轻轻按了按他的手臂，与其说是倚靠，不如说是扶持，说道：「告诉我吧」，坦然转向他，不带红晕、不带嗫嚅，端出一张扶持之爱的庄重而温柔的脸。

## XXXIX / 三十九
===Original===

Rolls disappeared on the evening of the day on which he had that long consultation with Mr. Monypenny. He did not return to Dalrulzian that night. Marget, with many blushes and no small excitement, served the dinner, which Bauby might be said to have cooked with tears. If these salt drops were kept out of her sauces, she bedewed the white apron which she lifted constantly to her eyes. “Maister John in jyal! and oor Tammas gone after him; and what will I say to his mammaw?” Bauby cried. She seemed to fear that it might be supposed some want of care on her part which had led to this dreadful result. But even the sorrow of her soul did not interfere with her sense of what was due to her master’s guest. Beaufort’s dinner did not suffer, whatever else might. It was scrupulously cooked, and served with all the care of which Marget was capable; and when it was all over, and everything carefully put aside, the women sat down together in the kitchen, and had a good cry over the desolation of the house. The younger maids, perhaps, were not so deeply concerned on this point as Bauby, who was an old servant, and considered Dalrulzian as her home: but they were all more or less affected by the disgrace, as well as sorry for the young master, who had “nae pride,” and always a pleasant word for his attendants in whatever capacity. Their minds were greatly affected, too, by the absence of Rolls. Not a man in the house but the stranger gentleman! It was a state of affairs which alarmed and depressed them, and proved, above all other signs, that a great catastrophe had happened. Beaufort sent for the housekeeper after dinner to give her such information as he thought necessary; and Bauby was supported to the door by her subordinates, imploring her all the way to keep up her heart. “You’ll no’ let on to the strange gentleman.” “Ye’ll keep up a good face, and no’ let him see how sair cast down ye are,” they said, one at either hand. There was a great deal of struggling outside the door, and some stifled sounds of weeping, before it was opened, and Bauby appeared, pushed in by some invisible agency behind her, which closed the door promptly as soon as she was within.

===Chinese===

罗尔斯与莫尼彭尼先生长谈了一番，当天傍晚就不见了踪影。那晚他没有回达尔鲁尔齐恩（Dalrulzian）。玛格丽特红着脸、激动得不行地端上了晚饭——这顿饭可以说是鲍比（Bauby）就着眼泪做的。纵然这些咸点点滴没落进她的汤汁里，她那张不断举起来拭眼的白围裙，可是湿了又湿。「约翰先生坐了牢！咱们的塔姆斯又跟了去；他妈妈问起来，叫我怎么说呀？」鲍比哭道。她似乎怕人家当是：这可怕的结果，是她照管上有了什么闪失才招来的。可她灵魂里的悲伤，并没有搅扰她对主人宾客应尽的分寸。别的一切尽可以出岔，博福特（Beaufort）的晚饭却不受亏待。饭菜做得一丝不苟，伺候得尽玛格丽特的全副细心；待一切收场、样样仔细归置停当，女人们便一齐坐在厨房里，为这宅子的荒凉好好哭了一场。年轻些的女仆，在这一节上或许不如鲍比痛切——她是老仆人，把达尔鲁尔齐恩当作自己的家——可她们个个都为这门庭的耻辱或多或少伤着心，也为那位「没一点架子」、对下人无论执什么差事总有一句好话的少东家难过。罗尔斯的失踪也大大搅动了她们的心思。宅子里除了那位外乡绅士，再没有一个男人！这样的局面叫她们又惊又丧，比什么征兆都更能证明：出了大祸了。饭后博福特叫人去请管家娘子，要把她必需知道的事告诉她；鲍比由手下人左右搀到门口，一路求她千万撑住心。「您可不能在生人绅士面前露出来。」「您得撑住一副好脸色，别叫他看出您心里多么往下沉，」她们一边一个地说。门外先是一阵大大的挣扎和几声压着的呜咽，门才开，鲍比出现了——被身后一股看不见的势力推进来，她一进门，那股势力立刻把门带上。

===Original===

She was not the important person Beaufort had expected to see; but as she stood there, with her large white apron thrown over her arm, and her comely countenance, like a sky after rain, lighted up with a very wan and uncertain smile, putting the best face she could upon it, Beaufort’s sympathy overcame the inclination to laugh which he might have felt in other circumstances, at the sight of her sudden entrance and troubled clinging to the doorway. “Good evening,” he said, “Mrs.﻿—” “They call me Bauby Rolls, at your service,” said Bauby, with a curtsey, and a suppressed sob. “Mrs. Rolls,” said Beaufort, “your master may not come home for a few days; he asked me to tell you not to be anxious; that he hoped to be back soon; that there was nothing to be alarmed about.” “Eh! and was he so kind as think upon me, and him in such trouble,” cried Bauby, giving way to her emotions. “But I’m no alarmt; no, no, why should I be?” she added, in a trembling voice. “He will be hame, no doubt, in a day or twa, as ye say, sir, and glad, glad we’ll a’ be. It’s not that we have any doubt﻿—but oh! what will his mammaw say to me?” cried Bauby. After the tremulous momentary stand she had made, her tears flowed faster than ever. “There has no such thing happened among the Erskines since ever the name was kent in the countryside, and that’s maist from the beginning, as it’s written in Scripture.” “It’s all a mistake,” cried Beaufort. “That it is﻿—that it is,” cried Bauby, drying her eyes. And then she added with another curtsey, “I hope you’ll find everything to your satisfaction, sir, till the maister comes hame. Tammas﻿—that’s the butler, Tammas Rolls, my brother, sir, if ye please﻿—is no’ at hame tonight, and you wouldna like a lass aboot to valet ye; they’re all young but me. But if you would put out your cloes to brush, or anything that wants doing, outside your door, it shall a’ be weel attended to. I’m real sorry there’s no’ another man aboot the house: but a’ that women can do we’ll do, and with goodwill.” “You are very kind, Mrs. Rolls,” said Beaufort. “I was not thinking of myself﻿—you must not mind me. I shall get on very well. I am sorry to be a trouble to you at such a melancholy moment.” “Na, na, sir, not melancholy,” cried Bauby, with her eyes streaming; “sin’ ye say, and a’body must allow, that it’s just a mistake: we manna be put aboot by suchlike trifles.

===Chinese===

她不是博福特料想中要见的那位要紧人物；可她站在那里，白围裙搭在臂上，一张端好的脸像雨后的天，亮着一副极苍白、极拿不稳的笑，竭力往好里撑——她的突然进门、她扒着门框的惶惶，博福特的同情压过了在别的情形下他也许会觉出的笑意。「晚上好，」他说，「罗——太太？」「人家叫我鲍比·罗尔斯，听您吩咐，」鲍比说着，行了个屈膝礼，压下一声呜咽。「罗尔斯太太，」博福特说，「您的主人这几天兴许回不了家；他托我告诉您，别焦急；他指望很快就回来；没有什么可惊慌的。」「唉！他自己那样身处麻烦，还想着我，多好啊，」鲍比喊道，情感决了堤。「可我不惊慌；不，不，我惊慌什么呢？」她颤着声补上一句。「他会回家的，不用说，一两天里，照您说的，先生；到那天，咱们大伙儿要多高兴有多高兴。倒不是咱们有什么疑心——可是哦！他妈妈要怎么问我呢？」鲍比喊道。那阵发颤的强撑撑过一时，她的眼泪比先前流得更凶了。「厄斯金家从没出过这样的事，打这名字在乡里有人知道起——那差不多是开天辟地起，白纸黑字写在《圣经》上的。」「这全是一场误会，」博福特喊道。「正是——正是，」鲍比喊道，擦干眼睛。随后她又行了个屈膝礼，添上一句：「盼您样样都满意，先生，等老爷回了家。塔姆斯——就是那位管家，塔姆斯·罗尔斯，我兄弟，您赏脸记着——今晚不在家，您总不肯叫个丫头进来伺候您换衣裳；除了我她们都年轻。可您要是把衣裳搁在门外头要刷，或有什么要办的，都会给您办得妥妥帖帖。宅子里没有第二个男人，我真心过意不去：可女人办得到的女人都办，还满心乐意。」「您太好了，罗尔斯太太，」博福特说。「我倒没有想着自己——您千万别把我放在心上。我会过得很好。这样伤心的时刻来给您添麻烦，抱歉得很。」「不，不，先生，不伤心，」鲍比喊道，眼泪直流；「既然您说了——大家也只得承认——这不过是一场误会：咱们可不能为这点子小事乱了阵脚。

===Original===

But nae doubt it will be livelier and mair pleesant for yoursel’, sir, when Mr. John and Tammas, they baith come hame. Would you be wanting anything more tonight?” “Na, I never let on,” Bauby said, when she retired to the ready support of her handmaidens outside the door﻿—“no’ me; I keepit a stout heart, and I said to him, ‘It’s of nae consequence, sir,’ I said﻿—‘I’m nane cast down; it’s just a mistake﻿—everybody kens that; and that he was to put his things outside his door,’ He got nothing that would go against the credit of the house out of me.”

But in spite of this forlorn confidence in her powers of baffling suspicion, it was a wretched night that poor Bauby spent. John was satisfactorily accounted for, and it was known where he was; but who could say where Rolls might be? Bauby sat up half through the night alone in the great empty kitchen with the solemn-sounding clock and the cat purring loudly by the fire. She was as little used to the noises of the night as Lord Rintoul was, and in her agony of watching felt the perpetual shock and thrill of the unknown going through and through her. She heard steps coming up to the house a hundred times through the night, and stealing stealthily about the doors. “Is that you, Tammas?” she said again and again, peering out into the night: but nobody appeared. Nor did he appear next day, or the next. After her first panic, Bauby gave out that he was with his master﻿—that she had never expected him﻿—in order to secure him from remark. But in her own mind horrible doubts arose. He had always been the most irreproachable of men; but what if, in the shock of this catastrophe, even Tammas should have taken to ill ways? Drink﻿—that was the natural suggestion. Who can fathom the inscrutable attractions it has, so that men yield to it who never could have been suspected of such a weakness? Most women of the lower classes have the conviction that no man can resist it. Heart-wrung for his master, shamed to his soul for the credit of the house, had Rolls, too, after successfully combating temptation for all his respectable life, yielded to the demon? Bauby trembled, but kept her terrors to herself. She said he might come back at any moment﻿—he was with his maister. Where else was it likely at such a time that he should be?

===Chinese===

「不过不用说，等约翰先生和塔姆斯两位都回了家，您这儿会更快活、更称心些，先生。今晚您还要什么吗？」「不，我什么也没露，」鲍比退到门外那班随时搀扶她的使女中间时说——「我才不呢；我撑住了一副硬心肠，我跟他说：『这算不得什么，先生，』我说——『我一点没往心里去；不过是一场误会——谁都明白；』还说了，请他把要刷的衣裳搁在门外头。从我嘴里，他没套走一句有损这宅子体面的话。」

可任凭她对自家遮掩的本事有这样孤苦的自信，可怜的鲍比那一夜过得凄惨。约翰的下落是交代清楚了，人人知道他在哪里；可谁能说罗尔斯在哪里？半夜里她独自坐在那间空荡荡的大厨房里，陪着她的是声气庄严的时钟和炉边大声打着呼噜的猫。她对夜里的种种声响，跟林图尔勋爵一样不惯；守夜的苦楚里，那未知的震动一阵阵穿透她全身。一夜里她一百次听见脚步朝宅子走来，又蹑手蹑脚绕着门口。「是你吗，塔姆斯？」她一遍遍朝夜色里张望发问：可没有人影。第二天他也没露面，第三天也没有。头一阵惊慌过后，鲍比对外放出话来，说他跟着主人呢——她本来就没想到他会回来——好堵住人的议论。可她自己心里升起了可怕的疑团。他一向是顶无可挑剔的人；可万一，这场大祸的震动，连塔姆斯也走了邪路呢？喝酒——那是头一个自然的想头。它那高深莫测的魅力，谁能参透？多少人一辈子没人疑心有这点软弱，竟也沉了进去。下层社会的女人多半有个定见：男人没有挡得住它的。为他的主人心都绞碎了，为宅子的体面羞到了灵魂深处——莫非罗尔斯也跟这魔鬼低头了，在体面了一辈子、一次次顶住了诱惑之后？鲍比发着抖，可把恐怖闷在自己肚里。她说他随时会回来——他在他老爷那儿。这样的时候，他还能在哪儿呢？

===Original===

But Rolls was not with his master. He was on the eve of a great and momentous act. There were no superstitious alarms about him, as about Rintoul, and no question in his mind what to do. Before he left Dalrulzian that sad morning, he had shaped all the possibilities in his thoughts, and knew what he intended; and his conversation with Mr. Monypenny gave substance and a certain reasonableness to his resolution. But it was not in his nature by one impetuous movement to precipitate affairs. He had never in his life acted hastily, and he had occasional tremors of the flesh which chilled his impulse and made him pause. But the interval, which was so bitter to his master, although all the lookers-on congratulated themselves it could do him no harm, was exactly what Rolls wanted in the extraordinary crisis to which he had come. A humble person, quite unheroic in his habits as in his antecedents, it was scarcely to be expected that the extraordinary project which had entered his mind should have been carried out with the enthusiastic impulse of romantic youth. But few youths, however romantic, would have entertained such a purpose as that which now occupied Rolls. There are many who would risk a great deal to smuggle an illustrious prisoner out of his prison. But this was an enterprise of a very different kind. He left Mr. Monypenny with his head full of thoughts which were not all heroic. None of his inquiries had been made without meaning. The self-devotion which was in him was of a sober kind, not the devotion of a Highland clansman, an Evan Dhu; and though the extraordinary expedient he had planned appeared to him more and not less alarming than the reality, his own self-sacrifice was not without a certain calculation and caution too.

可罗尔斯并不在他老爷那儿。他正临到一桩重大非常的举动的前夜。他身上没有林图尔那样的疑神疑鬼的惊惶，心里也不存「该怎么办」的问题。那个伤心的早晨离开达尔鲁尔齐恩之前，他已把一切可能在他脑子里定了形，拿稳了主意；与莫尼彭尼先生的一番话，又给他的决断添了实体和几分道理。可他的天性不是一步猛进、把事情推到头的人。他平生做事从不毛躁，何况血肉之躯时时有几分寒颤，叫他冲劲一冷、脚步一顿。可这段间歇——他的主人熬得那样苦，旁观的人却个个庆幸于他无伤——恰恰是罗尔斯在这场他走到跟前的大变局里求之不得的。一个卑微的人，习性履历都毫不英雄，谁能指望他心里那个异样的计划，会带着浪漫青春的热忱冲动去实行？可是任凭多浪漫的青年，也少有人怀过如今盘踞罗尔斯心里的这种图谋。冒着大险把一位显赫的囚徒偷渡出监牢，这样的事多的是人干。可他这一桩，是性质全然不同的功业。他离开莫尼彭尼先生时，满脑袋的念头并不全是英雄气。他打听的每一件事，没有一件是白问的。他身上的自我献身是素净的一路，不是高地氏族人那股热肠，不是埃文·杜；虽说他所筹的那条非常的出路，在他眼里愈想愈比方才的实情更骇人，他这份自我牺牲里也并非没有几分盘算和谨慎。

All these things had been seriously weighed and balanced in his mind. He had considered his sister’s interest, and even his own eventual advantage. He had never neglected these primary objects of life, and he did not do so now. But though all was taken into account and carefully considered, Rolls’s first magnanimous purpose was never shaken; and the use he made of the important breathing-time of these intervening days was characteristic. He had, like most men, floating in his mind several things which he intended “some time” to do﻿—a vague intention which, in the common course of affairs, is never carried out. One of these things was to pay a visit to Edinburgh. Edinburgh to Rolls was as much as London and Paris and Rome made into one. All his patriotic feelings, all that respect for antiquity which is natural to the mind of a Scot, and the pride of advancing progress and civilisation which becomes a man of this century, were involved in his desire to visit the capital of his own country. Notwithstanding all the facilities of travel, he had been there but once before, and that in his youth. With a curious solemnity he determined to make this expedition now. It seemed the most suitable way of spending these all-important days, before he took the step beyond which he did not know what might happen to him. A more serious visitor, yet one more determined to see everything and to take the full advantage of all he saw, never entered that romantic town. He looked like a rural elder of the gravest Calvinistic type as he walked, in his black coat and loosely tied white neckcloth, about the lofty streets. He went to Holyrood, and gazed with reverence and profound belief at the stains of Rizzio’s blood. He mounted up to the Castle and examined Mons Meg with all the care of a historical observer. He even inspected the pictures in the National Collection with unbounded respect, if little knowledge, and climbed the Observatory on the Calton Hill. There were many spectators about the streets who remarked him as he walked about, looking conscientiously at everything, with mingled amazement and respect; for his respectability, his sober curiosity, his unvarying seriousness, were remarkable enough to catch an intelligent eye.

===Chinese===

这一切，他都在心里郑重掂量过、平衡过。他盘算过妹妹的利益，甚至自己日后的好处。这些人生的首要目标他从没疏忽过，如今也没有。可纵然样样计入、细细想过，罗尔斯头一等的慷慨宗旨从没有动摇；他怎样利用这段要紧的喘息日子，也别具他的本色。像大多数人一样，他心里悬着几件「哪一天」要做的事——这种含糊的打算，照常理是永远不会兑现的。其中一件，就是去爱丁堡（Edinburgh）走一趟。对罗尔斯，爱丁堡抵得上伦敦、巴黎、罗马合在一处。他满腔的爱国之情，一个苏格兰人天生的敬老怀古，再加本世纪的人对进步文明的自豪，尽在这看一看自己国都的心愿里。旅途如今这样便利，他也统共去过一回，还是年轻时候。他怀着一种古怪的郑重，决意现在就作这一趟远征。这似乎是消磨这紧要几日的最合适的办法——跨出这一步之后，会出什么事，他不知道。再没有比这更严肃、又更决意要看遍一切、把所看的一分一毫都用足的游人，进过那座浪漫的城了。他穿一身黑外套，颈上松松系一条白围巾，走在那些高街上，活像一个顶严整的加尔文宗的乡村长老。他到荷里路德宫，怀着敬仰和全副的笃信，瞻仰里齐奥的血迹。他登上城堡，以历史观察家的全套细心察看「蒙斯·梅格」大炮。他甚至以无限的敬意——知识虽少——细看了国家收藏的那些画，还爬上了卡尔顿山的观象台。街上来往的看客不少，见他四处走动、样样都那么一本正经地看，又惊又敬；因为他那份体面、那份有节制的猎奇、那份一成不变的严肃，引人注目得很，瞒不过有眼力的人。

===Original===

But nobody suspected that Rolls’s visit to Edinburgh was the solemn visit of a martyr, permitting himself the indulgence of a last look at the scenes that interested him most, ere giving himself up to an unknown and mysterious doom.

On the morning of the 24th, having satisfied himself fully, he returned home. He was quite satisfied. Whatever might now happen, he had fulfilled his intention, and realised his dreams: nothing could take away from him the gratification thus secured. He had seen the best that earth contained, and now was ready for the worst, whatever that might be. Great and strange sights, prodigies unknown to his fathers, were befitting and natural objects to occupy him at this moment of fate. It was still early when he got back: he stopped at the Tinto Station, not at that which was nearest to Dalrulzian, and slowly making his way up by the fatal road, visited the scene of Torrance’s death. The lodge-keeper called out to him, as he turned that way, that the road was shut up; but Rolls paid no heed. He clambered over the hurdles that were placed across, and soon reached the scene of the tragedy. The marks of the horse’s hoofs were scarcely yet obliterated, and the one fatal point at which the terrified brute had dinted deeply into the tough clay, its last desperate attempt to hold its footing, was almost as distinct as ever.

The terrible incident with which he had so much to do came before him with a confused perception of things he had not thought of at the time, reviving, as in a dream, before his very eyes. He remembered that Torrance lay with his head down the stream﻿—a point which had not struck him as important; and he remembered that Lord Rintoul had appeared out of the wood at his cry for help so quickly, that he could not have been far away when the accident took place. What special signification there might be in these facts Rolls was not sufficiently clearheaded to see. But he noted them with great gravity in a little notebook, which he had bought for the purpose. Then, having concluded everything, he set out solemnly on his way to Dunearn.

===Chinese===

可谁也没有疑心，罗尔斯这趟爱丁堡之行，是一位殉道者的郑重巡礼——在把自己交出去领受未知的神秘劫数之前，容自己纵情最后看一眼他最牵挂的景物。

二十四号早晨，他心满意足了，便动身回家。他真是心满意足。如今无论出什么事，他的心愿已了，梦已圆：谁也夺不走这份既得的满足。人间的至好他见过了，如今的至坏，随它是什么，他都备下了。伟大奇异的景象，他的父辈闻所未闻的奇观，正当他命定的此刻来占据他的心神，也算相宜、也算自然。他到家时还早：他在廷托（Tinto）车站下的车——没有在离达尔鲁尔齐恩最近的那个站——沿着那条要命的路慢慢走上坡，去看了托伦斯（Torrance）丧命的地方。他拐上那条道时，看门人朝他喊，说路封了；罗尔斯不理会。他攀过横在路口的栅栏，不久便到了惨事的现场。马蹄的印子还几乎没磨灭；那一个要命的落点——那匹吓疯了的牲口在韧泥里深深踏出的最后一拼——还几乎跟先前一样分明。

那桩与他干系重大的惨事，带着他当时不曾想到的种种，恍恍惚惚来到他眼前，像一场梦，在他眼皮底下复活。他记起托伦斯躺卧时头朝着下游——这一点当时不曾被他看重；他又记起，他喊救的那一声刚出，林图尔勋爵就从树林里出来了，来得那样快，出事时他必在近处。这些事实里含着什么特别的意味，罗尔斯的头脑不够清明，看不出来。可他把它们极郑重地记进一本小小的记事簿——专为这桩事买的。随后，一切办完，他迈开郑重的步子，往邓恩（Dunearn）去了。

===Original===

It was a long walk. The autumnal afternoon closed in mists; the moon rose up out of the haze﻿—the harvest moon, with a little redness in her light. The landscape was dim in this mellowed vapour, and everything subdued. The trees, with all their fading glories, hung still in the haze; the river tinkled with a far-off sound; the lights in the cottages were blurred, and looked like huge vague lamps in the milky air, as Rolls trudged on slowly, surely, to the place of fate. It took him a long time to walk there, and he did not hurry. Why should he hurry? He was sure, went he ever so slowly, to arrive in time. As he went along, all things that ever he had done came up into his mind. His youthful extravagances﻿—for Rolls, too, had once been young and silly; his gradual settling into manhood; his aspirations, which he once had, like the best; his final anchorage, which, if not in a very exalted post, nor perhaps what he had once hoped for, was yet so respectable. Instead of the long lines of trees, the hedgerows, and cottages which marked the road, it was his own life that Rolls walked through as he went on. He thought of the old folk, his father and mother; he seemed to see Bauby and himself and the others coming home in just such a misty autumn night from school. Jock, poor fellow! who had gone to sea, and had not been heard of for years; Willie, who ’listed, and nearly broke the old mother’s heart. How many shipwrecks there had been among the lads he once knew! Rolls felt, with a warmth of satisfaction about his heart, how well it was to have walked uprightly, to have “won through” the storms of life, and to have been a credit and a comfort to all belonging to him. If anything was worth living for, that was. Willie and Jock had both been cleverer than he, poor fellows! but they had both dropped, and he had held on. Rolls did not want to be proud; he was quite willing to say, “If it had not been for the grace of God!﻿—” but yet it gave him an elevating sense of the far superior pleasure it was to conquer your inclinations in the days of your youth, and to do well whatever might oppose. When the name of Rolls was mentioned by anyone about Dunearn, it would always be said that two of them had done very well﻿—Tammas and Bauby: these were the two. They had always held by one another; they had always been respectable.

那是一段长长的路。秋日的午后合拢在雾里；月亮从雾霭中升起——收获月，光里带着一点红。景物在这层温软的水汽里朦朦胧胧，一切都低了声气。树木带着满身褪色的荣华，静静悬在雾里；河水叮咚，是远远的声响；农舍的灯火晕开了，在乳白的空气里像一盏盏巨大而模糊的灯——罗尔斯一步一步、稳稳当当，走向命定之地。这段路他走了很久，他也不赶。赶什么呢？他走得再慢，也笃定到得不误时辰。一路走着，他平生做过的事，一件件浮上心头。年轻时的荒唐——罗尔斯也曾年轻傻气过；他怎样渐渐落定成个男人；他曾经也有过的、不输最好之人的抱负；他最后的锚地——虽说不在什么高贵的位分上，或许也不及他当初指望的，却那样体面。一路的树列、篱垣、农舍，都退成了背景；罗尔斯走过的，是他自己的一生。他想起老人们，他的父亲母亲；他仿佛看见鲍比和他自己、还有弟妹们，在这样一个雾蒙蒙的秋夜从学堂回家。乔克，可怜的人！去了海上，多年没有音信；威利，从了军，差点要了老母亲的命。他早年认识的那些小子，翻船的有多少！罗尔斯心头发着一团暖洋洋的满足：一辈子行得正、「闯过」了人生的风波、叫所有亲眷面上有光、心里有靠，多好。若说有什么值得活着，那就为这个。威利和乔克当年都比他伶俐，可怜的人！可他们俩都跌落了，他撑住了。罗尔斯不想自负；他满愿意说一句「若不是上帝的恩典！」——可它到底给了他一种高升之感：年轻时降得住自己的欲念、顶得住一切引诱而做得端正，实在是远远高过一切的快乐。日后邓恩一带有人提起罗尔斯家的名字，总会说：他们家有两个出息的——塔姆斯和鲍比：就是这两位。他们一辈子相依相持；一辈子体面。

But here Rolls stopped in his thoughts, taking a long breath. After this, after what was going to happen, what would the folk say then? Would a veil drop after today upon the unblemished record of his life? He had never stood before a magistrate in all his days﻿—never seen how the world looked from the inside of a prison, even as a visitor﻿—had nothing to do, nothing to do with that side of the world. He waved his hand, as if separating by a mystic line between all that was doubtful or disreputable, and his own career. But now﻿—Thus through the misty darkening road, with now a red gleam from a smithy, and now a softer glimmer from a cottage door, and anon the trees standing out of the mists, and the landscape widening about him, Rolls came on slowly, very seriously, to Dunearn. The long tower of the Town House, which had seemed to threaten and call upon Lord Rintoul, was the first thing that caught the eye of Rolls. The moon shone upon it, making a white line of it against the cloudy sky.

想到这里，罗尔斯收住念头，长长吸了一口气。这以后——待那件要发生的事发生了——人家又该怎么说呢？今天过后，会不会有一幅帘子，落在他一生无瑕的记录上？他一辈子没在治安官跟前站过——连探监也没见识过牢里看世界是什么光景——与世界的那个侧面，毫无干系，毫无干系。他挥了挥手，仿佛在自己的一生与一切可疑、不体面的地段之间，划下一道神秘的界线。可如今——就这样，穿过雾气渐浓的路，忽而一处铁匠铺透出红光，忽而一处农舍门口泛出柔晕，时而有树木从雾里显出形来，景物在他身旁展开，罗尔斯慢慢走来，一路极郑重地，进了邓恩。镇公所那座长长的塔楼——先前在林图尔勋爵眼里像是威胁着、召唤着他的——头一个撞进罗尔斯的眼帘。月光照在塔上，把它照成一道白线，衬着多云的天。

Mr. Monypenny was at dinner with his family. They dined at six o’clock, which was thought a rather fashionable hour, and the comfortable meal was just over. Instead of wine, the good man permitted himself one glass of toddy when the weather grew cold. He was sitting between the table and the fire, and his wife sat on the other side giving him her company and consolation﻿—for Mr. Monypenny was somewhat low and despondent. He had been moved by Sir James Montgomery’s warm and sudden partisanship and belief of John Erskine’s story; but he was a practical man himself, and he could not, he owned, shaking his head, take a sensational view. To tell him that there should have been just such an encounter as seemed probable﻿—high words between two gentlemen﻿—but that they should part with no harm done, and less than an hour after one of them be found lying dead at the bottom of the Scaur﻿—that was more than he could swallow in the way of a story. To gain credence, there should have been less or more. Let him hold his tongue altogether﻿—a man is never called upon to criminate himself﻿—or let him say all. “Then you must just give him a word, my dear, to say nothing about it,” said Mrs. Monypenny, who was anxious too. “But that’s just impossible, my dear, for he blurted it all out to the sheriff just as he told it to me.” “Do you not think it’s a sign of innocence that he should keep to one story, and when it’s evidently against himself, so far as it goes?” “A sign of innocence!” Mr. Monypenny said, with a snort of impatience. He took his toddy very sadly, finding no exhilaration in it. “Pride will prevent him departing from his story,” he said. “If he had spoken out like a man, and called for help like a Christian, it would have been nothing. All this fuss is his own doing﻿—a panic at the moment, and pride﻿—pride now, and nothing more.”

“If ye please,” said the trim maid who was Mr. Monypenny’s butler and footman all in one﻿—the “table-maid,” as she was called﻿—“there’s one wanting to speak to ye, sir. I’ve put him into the office, and he says he can wait.”

“One! and who may the one be?” said Mr. Monypenny.

“Weel, sir, he’s got his hat doon on his brows and a comforter aboot his throat, and he looks sore for-foughten, as if he had travelled all the day, and no’ a word to throw at a dog; but I think it’s Mr. Rolls, the butler at Dalrulzian.”

莫尼彭尼先生正和家人用晚饭。他们六点开饭——这钟点被认为相当时髦——那顿舒坦的饭刚刚吃完。天冷了，这位好人容自己喝上一杯热酒，代替葡萄酒。他坐在桌子和炉火之间，太太坐在另一边作陪劝慰——因为莫尼彭尼先生有点消沉颓丧。詹姆斯·蒙哥马利爵士对约翰·厄斯金（John Erskine）说法那番热辣辣、突如其来的袒护和信任，打动了他；可他自己是个务实的人，他承认——摇着头——轰动式的看法他拿不出。对他说，确实有过一场似乎说得通的相遇——两位绅士言语冲突——却各自走开、毫发无伤，不出一个钟头，其中一个就死在斯考崖底下——这样的故事，他咽不下。要人信，总得再多一点或少一点。要么索性缄口——谁也无须自证其罪——要么和盘托出。「那你就得给他捎句话，亲爱的，叫他对这事一个字也别提，」莫尼彭尼太太说，她也焦心。「可那正办不到，亲爱的，他在郡法官跟前已经脱口全说了，跟我讲的一样。」「他咬定一个说法不放，而且明摆着于自己不利——你不觉得这正是不清白的凭据吗？」「不清白的凭据！」莫尼彭尼先生说，不耐烦地哼了一声。他那杯热酒喝得愁眉苦脸，一点不见酒意。「是骄傲不许他改口，」他说。「他当时要是像个男人那样喊出来，像个基督徒那样喊人救，本可以什么事都没有。这场风波全是他自家招的——当时一慌，随后是骄傲——如今是骄傲，仅此而已。」

「回您的话，」那个利落的女仆——她一身兼任莫尼彭尼家的管家和男仆，人称「桌边丫头」——进来说，「有位要跟您说话，先生。我把他让进账房了，他说他等得起。」

「一位！这一位会是谁呢？」莫尼彭尼先生说。

「这个，先生，他把帽子压到眉毛上，脖子上裹着条围脖，看去苦大仇深的，像走了一整天路，一句话也懒得多说；可我想是罗尔斯老板，达尔鲁尔齐恩的那位管家。」

“Rolls!” said Mr. Monypenny. “I’ll go to him directly, Jeanie. That’s one thing off my mind. I thought that old body had disappeared rather than bear witness against his master,” he said, when the girl had closed the door.

“But oh, if he’s going to bear witness against his master, it would have been better for him to disappear,” said the sympathetic wife. “Nasty body! to eat folk’s bread, and then to get them into trouble.”

“Whesht with your foolish remarks, my dear: that is clean against the law, and it would have had a very bad appearance, and prejudiced the Court against us,” Mr. Monypenny said as he went away. But to tell the truth, he was not glad; for Rolls was one of the most dangerous witnesses against his master. The agent went to his office with a darkened brow. It was not well lighted, for the lamp had been turned down, and the fire was low. Rolls rose up from where he had been sitting on the edge of a chair as Mr. Monypenny came in. He had unwound his comforter from his neck, and taken off his hat. His journey, and his troubled thoughts, and the night air, had limped and damped him; the starch was out of his tie, and the air of conscious rectitude out of his aspect. He made a solemn but tremulous bow, and stood waiting till the door was closed, and the man of business had thrown himself into a chair. “Well, Rolls﻿—so you have come back!” Mr. Monypenny said.

“Ay, sir, I’ve come back. I’ve brought you the man, Mr. Monypenny, that did *yon*.”

“Good Lord, Rolls! that did what? You take away my breath.”

“I’ll do it more or I’m done. The man that coupit yon poor lad Tinto and his muckle horse ower the brae.”

Mr. Monypenny started to his feet. “Do you mean to tell me﻿—Lord bless us, man, speak out, can’t ye! The man that﻿—Are ye in your senses, Rolls? And who may this man be?”

“You see before you, sir, one that’s nae better than a coward. I thought it would blow by. I thought the young master would be cleared in a moment. There was nae ill meaning in my breast. I did the best I could for him as soon as it was done, and lostna a moment. But my courage failed me to say it was me﻿—”

“You!” cried Monypenny, with a shout that rang through the house.

===Chinese===

「罗尔斯！」莫尼彭尼先生说。「我这就去，珍妮。这倒去了我一桩心事。我还当那老家伙是躲起来了，不肯出证对付他家老爷呢，」女仆关上门后，他说。

「可是哦，他要是当真要出证对付他家老爷，那他还不如躲了好，」富有同情的太太说。「脏东西！吃了人家的饭，回头又叫人家遭殃。」

「收起你这些糊涂话，亲爱的：那简直犯法，叫人看见了面子上也很难看，还要叫法庭先存了成见，」莫尼彭尼先生边走边说。可说实在的，他并不高兴；因为罗尔斯是对他家老爷顶危险的证人。这位代理人板着一副黑脸进了账房。屋里灯芯捻低了，火也弱，不很亮堂。莫尼彭尼先生进来时，罗尔斯从椅子边上站起身。他已把围脖解下，帽子摘了。一路的旅程、纷乱的心绪、夜里的寒气，叫他瘸了精神也打湿了他：领带上的浆性没了，脸上那副自觉端方的气也没了。他郑重而发颤地鞠了一躬，站着等门关严、等这位账房先生坐定。「好啊，罗尔斯——你到底回来了！」莫尼彭尼先生说。

「嗳，先生，我回来了。我把那个人给您带来了，莫尼彭尼先生，干*那桩事*的人。」

「老天爷，罗尔斯！干什么的？你叫我喘不上气了。」

「我还要叫您更喘不上，不然我就不算人。把那可怜的廷托少爷和他那大马掀下坡去的那个人。」

莫尼彭尼先生霍地站起。「你是要告诉我——老天保佑，老兄，说出来，行不行！那个人——你神志清醒吗，罗尔斯？这个人又会是谁？」

「您眼前站着的，先生，一个不比懦夫好多少的人。我原想这事会过去的。我原想少东家一霎时就没事了。我心里没有半点恶意。事情一出，我立时尽我所能照应了他，一刻没耽搁。可我的勇气短了一截，没能说出那是我——」

「你！」莫尼彭尼喊了出来，一声吼响彻了宅子。

===Original===

“Just me, and no other; and what for no’ me? Am I steel and airn, to take ill words from a man that was no master of mine? Ye can shut me up in your prison﻿—I meant him no hairm﻿—and hang me if you like. I’ll no’ let an innocent man suffer instead of me. I’ve come to give myself up.”

===Chinese===

「正是我，不是别人；为什么不该是我？难道我是钢是铁，受得住一个不是我主人的人的恶话？您尽管把我关进牢里——我没存心害他——喜欢的话把我绞死也行。我不肯叫一个无辜的人替我受过。我是来自首的。」

## XL / 四十
===Original===

“**Dear Mr. Erskine**﻿—I do not know what words to use to tell you how pained and distressed we are﻿—I speak for my mother as well as myself﻿—to find that nothing has been done to relieve you from the consequence of such a ridiculous as well as unhappy mistake. We found my brother Robin as anxious as we were, or more so, if that were possible, to set matters right at once; but unfortunately on the day after, the funeral took up all thoughts: and what other obstacles intervened next day I cannot rightly tell, but something or other﻿—I am too impatient and pained to inquire what﻿—came in the way; and they tell me now that tomorrow is the day of the examination, and that it is of no use now to forestall justice, which will certainly set you free tomorrow. Oh, dear Mr. Erskine, I cannot tell you how sick and sore my heart is to think that you have been in confinement (it seems too dreadful, too ludicrous, to be true), in confinement all these long days. I feel too angry, too miserable, to think of it. I have been crying, as if that would do you any good, and rushing up and down abusing everybody. I think that in his heart Robin feels it more than any of us: he feels the injustice, the foolishness; but still he has been to blame, and I don’t know how to excuse him. We have not dared to tell poor Carry﻿—though, indeed, I need not attempt to conceal from you, who have seen so much, that poor Carry, though she is dreadfully excited and upset, is not miserable, as you would expect a woman to be in her circumstances. Could it be expected? But I don’t know what she might do if she heard what has happened to you. She might take some step of her own accord, and that would be not prudent, I suppose; so we don’t tell her. Oh, Mr. Erskine, did you ever think how miserable women are? I never realised it till now. Here am I, and, still more, here is my mother. She is not a child, or an incapable person, I hope! yet she can do nothing﻿—nothing to free you. She is as helpless as if she were a baby. It seems to me ridiculous that Robin’s opinion should be worth taking, and mine not; but that is quite a different matter. My mother can do nothing but persuade and plead with a boy like Robin, to do that which she herself, at her age, wise as she is, good as she is, cannot do.

===Chinese===

**亲爱的厄斯金先生**——我不知道该用什么话告诉您，得知竟没有采取任何措施让您从这样一个又荒唐又不幸的错误的后果里脱身，我们心里多么难过、多么不安——我是替母亲、也替我自己说的。我们发现我哥哥罗宾跟我们一样着急——若还有过之——想立刻把事情扳正；可是不巧，第二天葬礼占去了全部心思：再隔一天又有什么别的阻碍从中作梗，我说不清；反正有什么事——我急得、痛得顾不上问是什么——挡了道；如今他们告诉我，明天就是过堂的日子，说现在再去抢先已没有用处，正义明天必然会还您自由。啊，亲爱的厄斯金先生，一想到您竟被关押着（这事太可怕、也太荒唐，简直不像真的），这么多漫长的日子一直关押着，我说不出我心里有多酸痛。我一想起来就愤怒，就难过。我哭了一场，仿佛哭能帮到您似的，又跑上跑下把人人骂了一遍。我想罗宾心里比我们谁都难受：他觉出这不公道、这愚蠢；可他毕竟难辞其咎，我不知道该怎么替他开脱。我们一直不敢告诉可怜的卡丽——不过说真的，在您这样明察一切的人面前，我也不必试图隐瞒：可怜的卡丽虽然激动伤心得厉害，却并不像您以为处在她那境地的女人那样悲苦。这能指望吗？可我不知道她若听说您的遭遇会做出什么来。她也许会自作主张采取什么行动，我想那就不明智了；所以我们不告诉她。啊，厄斯金先生，您可曾想过女人多么可怜？我直到如今才明白过来。想想我，更想想我母亲。她不是小孩子，也不是无能的人，我希望！可她什么都做不了——救不了您。她无助得像个婴孩。依我看真是荒唐：罗宾的意见值得采纳，我的就不值；不过那完全是另一码事。我母亲什么都做不了，只能去劝、去恳求罗宾这样一个孩子，去做她本人——以她的年纪、她的智慧、她的善良——自己做不到的事。

===Original===

As you are a man, you may think this of no importance; and mamma says it is nature, and cannot be resisted, and smiles. But if you suppose she does not feel it!﻿—if she could have been your bail, or whatever it is, you may be sure you would not have been a single night in *that* place! but all that we can do is to go down on our knees to the men who have it in their power, and I, unfortunately, have not been brought up to go down on my knees. Forgive me for this outburst. I am so miserable to think where you are, and why, and that I﻿—I mean *we*﻿—can do nothing. What can I say to you? Dear Mr. Erskine, our thoughts are with you constantly. My mother sends you her love.

“Edith.”

===Chinese===

您是男人，也许觉得这无关紧要；妈妈说这是天性，抗拒不得，还笑了笑。可您要是以为她不往心里去！——倘若她能做您的保人，或是别的什么名目，您准保连一夜都不会进那个地方！可我们所能做的，只有向那些有权的人屈膝下跪，而不巧的是，我受的教养没教过我下跪。原谅我这一番发作。一想到您在哪里、为什么、而我——我是说我们——无能为力，我就难过极了。我还能对您说什么呢？亲爱的厄斯金先生，我们的心时刻和您在一起。母亲向您致以她的爱。

伊迪丝

===Original===

Edith felt perhaps that this was not a very prudent letter. She was not thinking of prudence, but of relieving her own mind and comforting John Erskine, oppressed and suffering. And besides, she was herself in a condition of great excitement and agitation. She had been brought back from Tinto, she and her mother, with a purpose. Perhaps it was not said to her in so many words; but it was certainly conveyed to the minds of the female members of the family generally that Millefleurs was at the end of his patience, and his suit must have an answer once for all. Carry had been told of the proposal by her mother, and had pledged herself to say nothing against it. And she had kept her promise, though with difficulty, reserving to herself the power to act afterwards if Edith should be driven to consent against her will. “Another of us shall not do it,” Carry said; “oh, not if I can help it!” “I do not believe that Edith will do it,” said Lady Lindores; “but let us not interfere﻿—let us not interfere!” Carry, therefore, closed her mouth resolutely; but as she kissed her sister, she could not help whispering in her ear, “Remember that I will always stand by you﻿—always, whatever happens!” This was at Lindores, where Carry, pining to see once more the face of the outer world since it had so changed to her, drove her mother and sister in the afternoon, returning home alone with results which were not without importance in her life. But in the meantime it is Edith with whom we have to do. She reached home with the sense of having a certain ordeal before her﻿—something which she had to pass through, not without pain﻿—which would bring her into direct antagonism with her father, and convulse the household altogether. Even the idea that she must more or less vex Millefleurs distressed and excited her; for indeed she was quite willing to admit that she was “very fond of” Millefleurs, though it was ridiculous to think of him in any other capacity than that of a brotherly friend. And it was at this moment she made the discovery that, notwithstanding the promises of Rintoul and Millefleurs, nothing had been done for John.

===Chinese===

伊迪丝也许自己也觉出，这封信写得不算审慎。她想的不是审慎，而是吐一吐胸中块垒，安慰安慰受压制、受磨难的约翰·厄斯金。再说，她自己也正处于极大的激动与不安之中。她和母亲被人从廷托接了回来，是带着目的的。也许没有人对她明明白白说过；但家里的女性成员心里都确凿地得到了这个印象：米勒弗勒的耐心已到尽头，他的求婚必须有个一劳永逸的答复。母亲已把这门亲事告诉了卡丽，卡丽也保证不说反对的话。她守住了诺言，虽然很吃力，同时给自己保留了后手：倘若伊迪丝被逼得违心应允，她再相机行事。「我们中间不该再有第二个，」卡丽说；「啊，只要我拦得住，就不许有第二个！」「我不信伊迪丝会应，」林多雷斯夫人说；「可是咱们别插手——咱们别插手！」于是卡丽坚决闭上了嘴；可她吻妹妹时，还是忍不住附在她耳边低语：「记住，我永远站在你这边——永远，不管出什么事！」这是在林多雷斯。卡丽自从外面的世界对她变了脸，一心想再看看世面，午后便驾车送母亲和妹妹过去，独自回家——此行的结果，在她一生中并非无关紧要。但眼下要说的还是伊迪丝。她回到家里，自觉面前摆着一场考验——一件不得不熬过去的事，熬得不会不痛——它将使她与父亲正面顶撞，叫全家天翻地覆。就连或多或少要惹恼米勒弗勒这一层，也让她又难过又激动；因为说真的，她十分乐意承认自己「很喜欢」米勒弗勒，尽管要把他往兄长般的朋友以外的身份上去想，未免可笑。也正是在这个当口，她发现：尽管林图尔和米勒弗勒都许过诺，为约翰做的却什么都没有。

===Original===

The consequence was, that the letter which we have just quoted was at once an expression of sympathy, very warm, and indeed impassioned﻿—more than sympathy, indignation, wrath, sentiments which were nothing less than violent﻿—and a way of easing her own excited mind which nothing else could have furnished. “I am going to write to John Erskine,” she said, with the boldness produced by so great a crisis; and Lady Lindores had not interfered. She said, “Give him my love,” and that was all. No claim of superior prudence, or even wisdom, has been made for Lady Lindores. She had to do the best she could among all these imperfections. Perhaps she thought that, having expressed all her angry glowing heart to John, in the outflowing of impassioned sympathy, the girl would be more likely, in the reaction and fear lest she had gone too far, to be kind to Millefleurs; for who can gauge the ebbings and flowings of these young fantastic souls? And as for Lady Lindores’s private sentiments, she would not have forced her daughter a hairbreadth; and she had a good deal of pain to reconcile herself to Millefleurs’s somewhat absurd figure as the husband of Edith. But yet, when all is said, to give your child the chance of being a duchess, who would not sacrifice a little? If only Edith could make up her mind to it! Lady Lindores went no further. Nevertheless, when the important moment approached, she could not help, like Carry, breathing a word in her child’s ear, “Remember, there is no better heart in existence,” she said. “A woman could not have a better man.” Edith, in her excitement, grasped her mother’s arms with her two hands; but all the answer she gave was a little nervous laugh. She had no voice to reply.

===Chinese===

于是，我们方才引用的那封信，既是一份同情——非常热烈、简直是炽烈的同情——又不止是同情，还有愤慨、有怒火，种种激烈得无以复加的情绪——同时也是给她自己那颗沸腾的心寻的一条出路，旁的什么都不能替代。「我要给约翰·厄斯金写信，」她说，带着如此大变故激出来的胆气；林多雷斯夫人没有拦。她只说了一句：「替我问候他。」仅此而已。本书从不声称林多雷斯夫人有如何过人的审慎，乃至智慧。她只能在这一切的不圆满中间尽力而为。也许她想的是：姑娘既已把满腔怒火和热肠向着约翰倾泻净尽，等心潮回落、生怕自己过了头，反倒更可能善待米勒弗勒；谁能测得准这些年轻奇想的心潮涨落呢？至于林多雷斯夫人自家的心思，她绝不肯逼女儿一头发丝的距离；要把米勒弗勒那副有些滑稽的身段认作伊迪丝的丈夫，她也着实费了一番痛楚才勉强咽下。可是，说到底，能给自己的孩子一个当公爵夫人的机会，谁不肯牺牲一点呢？只要伊迪丝肯拿定主意！林多雷斯夫人没有再往前一步。然而等重要时刻临近，她也像卡丽一样，忍不住在女儿耳边吐出一句：「记住，天底下再没有比这更好的心了，」她说。「女人嫁不到更好的男人了。」伊迪丝激动之下，双手抓住母亲的手臂；可她全部的回答只是一声紧张的轻笑。她连出声回答的嗓子都没有了。

===Original===

“You will remember, Millefleurs, that my daughter is very young﻿—and﻿—and shy,” said Lord Lindores, on the other side. He was devoured by a desire to say, “If she refuses you, never mind﻿—I will make her give in;” which indeed was what he had said in a kind of paraphrase to Torrance. But Millefleurs was not the sort of person to whom this could be said. He drew himself up a little, and puffed out his fine chest, when his future father-in-law (as they hoped) made this remark. If Edith was not as willing to have him as he was to have her, she was not for Millefleurs. He almost resented the interference. “I have no doubt that Lady Edith and I will quite understand each other﻿—whichever way it may be,” Millefleurs added with a sigh, which suited the situation. As a matter of fact, he thought there could not be very much doubt as to the reply. It was not possible that they could have made him stay only to get a refusal at the end﻿—and Millefleurs was well aware that the girls were very few who could find it in their hearts to refuse a future dukedom: besides, had it not been a friendship at first sight﻿—an immediate liking, if not love? To refuse him now would be strange indeed. It was not until after dinner that the fated moment came. Neither Lord Lindores nor Rintoul came into the drawing-room; and Lady Lindores, having her previous orders, left the field clear almost immediately after the entrance of the little hero. There was nothing accidental about it, as there generally is, or appears to be, about the scene of such events. The great drawing-room, all softly lighted and warm, was never abandoned in this way in the evening. Edith stood before the fire, clasping her hands together nervously, the light falling warm upon her black dress and the gleams of reflection from its jet trimmings. They had begun to talk before Lady Lindores retreated to the background to look for something, as she said; and Millefleurs allowed the subject they were discussing to come to an end before he entered upon anything more important. He concluded his little argument with the greatest propriety, and then he paused and cleared his throat.

===Chinese===

「你要记住，米勒弗勒，我女儿很年轻——而且——而且怕生。」另一边，林多雷斯勋爵这样说。他心里被一句话啃噬着，很想脱口而出：「她若拒绝你，别在意——我会叫她让步的；」这话他当初对托伦斯其实就是换了个说法说过的。可米勒弗勒不是能对他说这种话的人。这位（如众人所盼的）未来岳父说出那句话时，他微微挺了挺身子，鼓起他饱满的胸脯。倘若伊迪丝嫁他不像他娶她那般情愿，那她就不要伊迪丝了——不，那她就不是配米勒弗勒的人。他对这干预几乎要生起气来。「我毫不怀疑，伊迪丝小姐和我会彼此十分了解——无论结果如何。」米勒弗勒补了一句，叹了口气，叹得正合时宜。事实上，他认为答复不会有多少悬念。人家不可能留他住下、到头来只为吃一个闭门羹——米勒弗勒也深知，能狠下心拒绝一个未来公爵夫人大位的姑娘屈指可数：何况，那不正是一见如故的交情——即便不是爱情，也是立时的好感？此刻拒绝他，那才真是咄咄怪事。直到晚饭之后，那个注定的时刻才到来。林多雷斯勋爵和林图尔都没有进客厅；林多雷斯夫人得了先前的吩咐，在那位小英雄进门之后不多时便腾清了场地。这里头没有半点凑巧——这类场面照例总要显得像是偶然。灯火柔和、暖意融融的大客厅，晚间从不这样空过。伊迪丝站在炉火前，紧张地合着双手，暖光落在她的黑裙上，落在黑玉镶边的点点反光上。林多雷斯夫人退到后头去找什么东西——她如是说——之前，两人已经攀谈起来；米勒弗勒也让正在谈的话题自然收了尾，才着手进行更要紧的事。他一丝不苟地结束了他的小议论，然后顿了顿，清了清嗓子。

===Original===

“Lady Edith,” he said, “you may not have noticed that we are alone.” He folded his little hands together, and put out his chest, and made all his curves more remarkable, involuntarily, as he said this.
