“With those eyes ye may be sure there’s no harm,” said Sir James, growing enthusiastic. “And I like the lad that had the sense to see what was in my little Nora. She’ll make a bonny countess, and I wish she was here that I might give her a kiss and tell her so. But this Lady Edith is a bonny creature too; and as for Lord Lindores himself, he’s no stranger, you know﻿—he’s just little Robby Lindores that both you and me mind. The one that has raised a prejudice, I make no doubt, is just that foreign wife of his﻿—”

“She is not foreign that ever I heard﻿—”

“Well, well﻿—maybe not according to the letter; but she has foreign ways, and without doubt it is her influence that has kept the family from settling down as we had a right to expect. My Lady Rintoul will set that right again. Bless me, who would have thought that little Nora﻿—But we must let bygones be bygones, Miss Barbara. We must just stand up for the young couple, and defeat the machinations of the foreign wife.”

===Chinese===

「长着那样一双眼，管保坏不到哪儿去，」詹姆斯爵士说，兴致高了起来。「我喜欢那小子，有眼力，识得我的小诺拉的好。她会是一位体面的伯爵夫人，恨不能她就在跟前，让我亲她一口，当面告诉她。不过这位伊迪丝小姐也是个俊俏人儿；至于林多雷斯勋爵本人，他可不是生人，你知道——他就是咱们俩都记得的小罗比·林多雷斯。惹起这一层偏见的，我拿准了，正是他那位外国太太——」

「我可从没听说她是外国人——」

「好好——照字面说兴许不是；可她一身洋派头，毫无疑问，正是她的势儿压着这一家，叫他们没能像咱们有权指望的那样落地生根。林图尔夫人来了自会拨乱反正。天哪，谁想得到小诺拉——不过过去的就让它过去吧，芭芭拉小姐。咱们只消替这对年轻人撑腰，破掉那位外国太太的好计。」

===Original===

Sir James laughed at this fine sentence of his; but yet he meant it. And even Miss Barbara agreed that this stranger woman was no doubt at the bottom of the mischief. When Sir James departed, the old lady felt herself nerved to a great exertion. By this time it was winter, and she went out but seldom, the pony-chaise being a cold conveyance. But that night she electrified her household by ordering the “carriage”﻿—the old carriage, never produced but on occasions of great solemnity﻿—for the next day. “Where will ye be going?” Janet asked, open-mouthed, after she had got over the shock of the announcement. But her mistress did not condescend to give her any answer. It was through Agnes, at a later hour, that information descended upon the household. “Sae far as I can make out, she is just going to Lindores to settle a’ about thae two marriages,” Agnes said in great excitement. “What two marriages? Ye think of nothing but marriages,” said Janet. But nevertheless that excellent person was as much excited as anyone when the huge vehicle drew up at the door next morning, and stood out in the rain to hear the orders which were given to the coachman. Agnes, seated within in attendance on her mistress, gave her a little nod with her eyelids, as much as to say, Who’s in the right now? “To Lindores.” “Bless me!” said Janet, “single women are aye so keen on that subject. They would ken better if they had ever had a man o’ their ain.”

===Chinese===

詹姆斯爵士被自己的漂亮句子逗笑了；可他倒真是这个意思。连芭芭拉小姐也附和说，闯下这祸的根子，多半就在这个外来女人身上。爵士走后，老太太自觉鼓起了一股干大事的劲。这时已是冬天，她轻易不出门，小马车那种交通工具又冷。可当晚她便下令明天用「大马车」——那辆老马车，不到大隆重的场合从不露面——把全家惊得目瞪口呆。「您要上哪儿去？」珍妮特缓过这惊讶之后，张着嘴问。可女主人不屑于答她。过了一个时辰，消息才经阿格尼丝之口降临全家。「照我咀摸，她就是要上林多雷斯，把那两桩婚事一总办妥。」阿格尼丝万分激动地说。「哪两桩婚事？你就知道婚事。」珍妮特说。可等到第二天早晨那辆庞然大物停到门口，这位可敬的人也激动得不亚于谁，冒着雨站在外头听吩咐车夫的话。阿格尼丝坐在车里侍候女主人，朝她眨了眨眼皮，等于说：谁说得准来着？「去林多雷斯。」「天哪！」珍妮特说，「单身女人对这桩事永远这样起劲。她们要是自己有过男人，就明白多了。」

===Original===

And indeed Miss Barbara’s magnificent intention was to make a proposal to Lord Lindores, which must, she could not doubt, make everything smooth. Lord Lindores was a gentleman, and took pains not to show the old lady, to whom the credit of the house of Dalrulzian was so dear, that he did not think the Erskines good enough to mate with his family: which was also a laudable exercise of discretion; for Miss Barbara was very strong in dates, and knew when the earldom of Lindores was founded, and who was the first of the family, as well as the exact period when the Erskines were settled at Dalrulzian. Lord Lindores forbore, partly out of good feeling, partly from alarm, and partly because Miss Barbara’s offer was not one to be refused. If it should so happen that he might be compelled to give in, then the settlement upon Edith of Miss Barbara’s fortune would make a very distinct difference in the case. He did not intend to give in, but still﻿—The proposal was received with great politeness at least. “There are many things to be taken into consideration,” he said. “I had other plans﻿—You will excuse me if I cannot give up my intentions in a moment, because two young people have chosen to fall in love with each other﻿—” “It is what we all have to do, my lord,” said Miss Barbara, who was old-fashioned, and gave every man his title. “It is the only thing, in my experience, that it is useless to fight against.” Then Lord Lindores made her a fine bow, and declared that this was a most appropriate sentiment from a lady’s lips; but a man must be excused if he took a graver view. There was a sharp accent in his voice which not all his politeness could quite disguise. “For my part,” Miss Barbara said, “I have just had to swallow my own disappointment, and think nothing of it; for what I had set my heart upon was to wed my nephew John to Nora Barrington, that now it appears, in the arrangements of Providence, is to be your lordship’s daughter-in-law, my Lady Rintoul.” Lord Lindores jumped up at this as if a knife had been put into him. He could scarcely trust himself to speak. “I can’t allow it to be an arrangement of Providence,” he cried bitterly, but recovered himself, and forced a smile upon his angry countenance, and assured Miss Barbara that her proposal was most generous.

===Chinese===

而芭芭拉小姐的宏图，也确是要向林多雷斯勋爵提一项提案——她毫不怀疑，这一提必定万事平顺。林多雷斯勋爵到底是位绅士，刻意不让老太太看出他嫌厄斯金家配不上自家门第——达尔鲁尔齐恩门楣的体面，于她是何等珍贵——这也不失为一种可嘉的审慎；因为芭芭拉小姐于年代掌故极有根底，林多雷斯的伯爵爵位立于何年、家族的第一人是谁、厄斯金家定居达尔鲁尔齐恩又在哪一朝哪一代，她一清二楚。林多雷斯勋爵忍住了，一半出于好意，一半出于忌惮，还有一半是因为芭芭拉小姐的提议本就不是可以回绝的那种。倘若当真到了不得不让步的一步，那么芭芭拉小姐的家财落在伊迪丝名下，这案子的分量便大不相同。他并不打算让步，可是——那项提案至少被极客气地接下了。「有许许多多方面要考虑，」他说。「我原有别的打算——两个年轻人自家要相恋，我便不能即刻放弃我的意图，这一点还望您见谅——」「这不正是人人免不了的么，勋爵。」芭芭拉小姐说——她守着老派规矩，对人人称足头衔。「依我一生的经验，这是唯一顶不住的东西。」于是林多雷斯勋爵朝她漂亮地一躬，声称出自女士之口，这话再得体不过；只是男子把事情看得郑重些，也请多多包涵。他嗓音里有一丝尖刻，再多的客气也遮不尽。「至于我，」芭芭拉小姐说，「我自家那点失望，也只好咽下去，不放在心上；我一心指望的，原是把我侄儿约翰配给诺拉·巴林顿——如今看来，按上天的安排，她要做勋爵大人的儿媳、林图尔夫人了。」林多雷斯勋爵闻言霍地跳起，仿佛身上被捅了一刀。他几乎信不过自己的嗓子。「我不容许这是上天的安排。」他愤然喊道，随即强自按捺，在愠怒的脸上挤出一副笑，向芭芭拉小姐保证，她的提议慷慨之至。

===Original===

He gave her his arm to the drawing-room, in which Lady Lindores and Edith were sitting, and withdrew, with his face drawn into a certain wolfish expression which his wife was aware meant mischief, but without betraying himself in speech. When he got back to his library, he launched a private anathema at the “old witch” who had taken it upon herself to interfere. But nevertheless, in Lord Lindores’ mind there arose the conviction that though he never would consent, yet if he did﻿—why, that Miss Barbara and her proposal were worth making a note of: and he did so accordingly. Miss Barbara, on her part, left the Castle half affronted, half mollified. She was angry that her proposal did not settle everything in a moment; but she was touched by the sweetness of Edith, and a little moved out of her prejudices in respect to Lady Lindores. “She has no foreign accent,” she said suddenly, in the midst of the drive, to the astonishment of Agnes﻿—“no more than any of us. And she has none of that sneering way﻿—my lord yonder, he just cannot contain himself for spite and illwill﻿—but I cannot see it in her. No doubt she’s one of them that is everybody’s body, and puts on a fine show﻿—but nothing from the heart.”

===Chinese===

他伸出手臂送她到客厅——林多雷斯夫人和伊迪丝正坐在那里——随后退了出去，脸绷出几分狼相；他妻子深知这神色主着祸事，他嘴里却一字不露。回到书房，他私下里把那多管闲事的「老妖婆」咒了一顿。然而在林多雷斯勋爵心里，到底生出了一个定见：虽然他永远不容应，可倘若——万一——容应了呢，那么这位芭芭拉小姐和她的提案，值得记上一笔：他果然记下了。芭芭拉小姐那边，离开城堡时半恼半慰。她的提案没能一锤定音，这叫她生气；可伊迪丝的甜美打动了她，对林多雷斯夫人的成见也被松动了几分。「她没有外国口音，」归途中她突然说，把阿格尼丝吓了一跳——「一点也不比咱们多。也没有那种嗤笑人的做派——咱们那位老爷，怨毒刻薄得简直存不住——可在她身上我看不见。不用说她也是那种人人跟前都应酬得到、场面摆得漂漂亮亮的人——可是没有一句是从心里出来的。」

===Original===

Some time after this another incident, which had no small bearing upon the story of one of these young pairs, occurred at Dalrulzian. Rintoul had never concealed his opposition, but neither had it ever become a subject of personal conflict between John Erskine and himself. He had gone away after his own explanation, for time did not stand still while these events were going on, and even a Guardsman has periods of duty. Shortly after he returned to Lindores, some question about the boundaries of the estates made it expedient that there should be formal communications between the two houses. Rintoul undertook to be the messenger. He had been with his regiment for the last two months, and he had not inquired into local events. He was, therefore, not in the least prepared for the sight that encountered him when he knocked at John Erskine’s door. It was opened to him by Rolls, in all the glory of shining “blacks” and snowy neckcloth, as composed, as authoritative, as fully in command of himself and everything about him, as he had ever been. Rintoul, though he was a lord and a soldier and a fine fellow, gave a jump backwards, which scattered the gravel on the path. “Good lord, Rolls!” he cried. It was not an agreeable surprise. He had done his best to forget Rolls, and he had succeeded. To have so many painful associations thus recalled was unpleasant; and the sight of him, so suddenly, without warning, an undeniable shock.

“Ay, my lord, it’s just Rolls,” said the butler, barring, as it were, his entrance. Rolls regarded the young man with a stern air; and even when Rintoul, recovering himself, began to express pleasure at his return, and great interest in hearing how it was, the face of Rolls remained unmoved. He changed his mind, however, about barring the entrance, and slowly showed Rintoul into the vacant dining-room, which he entered after him, shutting the door.

“I’ll easy tell your lordship how I got out,” he said; “but there’s mair pressing matter in hand. They tell me, my lord, that ye will not yield to have my maister, John Erskine of Dalrulzian, for Lady Edith’s man. I would like to hear if that’s true.”

“It’s a curious sort of question to ask,” said Rintoul. “I might ask what’s that to you, Rolls?”

===Chinese===

此后过了一些时日，达尔鲁尔齐恩又出了一桩事，于这对年轻人中一位的故事，干系不小。林图尔从不掩饰他的反对，但它也从未变成他同约翰·厄斯金之间的正面冲突。他表白过自己的道理便走了——这边诸事纷纷，时日却并不停摆，禁卫军人也有轮值当差的时候。他回林多雷斯后不久，两家田产地界上的一桩疑问，使得两宅之间必须有一番正式往来。林图尔揽下了传话的差事。他随团队待了两个月，没有打听地方上的事。因此，敲开约翰·厄斯金家门时撞见的那个景象，他毫无半点防备。开门的是罗尔斯，一身亮闪闪的黑礼服、雪白的领巾，威风十足，那份镇静、那份权威、那份对自己和周围一切的全盘掌控，一如往昔。林图尔虽是勋爵、是军人、是条好汉，也倒退了一大步，踏散了小径上的碎石。「我的老天，罗尔斯！」他喊道。这可不是什么愉快的意外。他一直尽力忘掉罗尔斯，而且忘得很成功。这么多痛楚的旧关联就这样被勾了回来，很不是滋味；而他这样突然地、毫无预警地现身，无可否认是一记震撼。

「嗳，老爷，正是罗尔斯。」管家说，那架势等于是拦着门。罗尔斯神情严正地打量这位年轻人；连林图尔回过神来、开始对他的归来表示高兴、表示极想知道原委时，罗尔斯的脸也纹丝不动。不过拦门的主意他改了，慢慢引林图尔进了空着的餐厅，自己随后进去，关上门。

「我是怎么出来的，回头轻易就告诉老爷您，」他说；「可眼下有更火烧眉毛的事。人家告诉我，老爷，您不肯点头，不肯让我的主人、达尔鲁尔齐恩的约翰·厄斯金做伊迪丝小姐的男人。我想听听，这是不是真的。」

「你这问题问得可够新鲜，」林图尔说。「我倒要问问，这与你何干，罗尔斯？」

===Original===

“Ay, so ye might﻿—it would be just like you, my lord; but I do not think it would be politic in all the circumstances. What for are you opposing it? Ye’re to marry Miss Nora, and get your ain will and pleasure. I wish her much joy, poor thing, and strength of mind to bear a’ that’s before her. What is your lordship’s objection to my maister, if I may make so bold as to ask?”

“You are not very complimentary,” said Rintoul, growing red.

“No, I’m no’ complimentary, my lord; it’s no’ my line. Will you tell me what’s set you against this marriage? for that is what I would like to ken.”

Rintoul tried to laugh, though it would have pleased him better to knock his monitor down. “You must see, Rolls, that a thing like this is my own concern,” he said.

“It’s my concern as well,” said Rolls. “There’s mair between you and me, my lord, than I’m wanting to tell; but if I was in your lordship’s place, I would not rin counter to them that has proved themselves your best friend﻿—”

“Rolls! what are you doing here?” cried John Erskine, with amazement, suddenly opening the door.

The countenance of Rolls was quite impassive. “I was giving my Lord Rintoul an account of my marvellous deliverance out o’ my prison, sir,” he said, “and how it was thought I had suffered enough in my long wait for the trial. And that was true. Much have I suffered, and many a thought has gone through my head. I’m real ripened in my judgment, and awfu’ well acquaint with points o’ law. But I hope I may never have anything more ado with such subjects﻿—if it be not upon very urgent occasion,” Rolls said. And he withdrew with a solemn bow to Rintoul, in his usual methodical and important way.

===Chinese===

「嗳，您尽管问——问出来才像您呢，老爷；可依我看，眼下这情形，问得不聪明。您拦这门亲做什么？您自个儿要娶诺拉小姐，自个儿的意愿自个儿遂。我愿她多多欢喜，可怜的人，也愿她有心力担得起前头的一切。恕我斗胆问一句，老爷，您对我主人到底有什么不满？」

「你嘴下可不留情。」林图尔说，红了脸。

「是，我不留情，老爷；留情不是我的行当。您肯不肯告诉我，是什么叫您拦着这桩婚事？这正是我想知道的。」

林图尔勉强笑了笑，虽说更称心的做法是把这位谅友打翻在地。「你该明白，罗尔斯，这样的事是我自己的事。」他说。

「也是我的事。」罗尔斯说。「您我之间的事，老爷，比我愿意说出口的多得多；可我要是处在老爷您的位置，我决不去顶撞那些证明了自个儿是您最好的朋友的人——」

「罗尔斯！你怎么在这儿？」约翰·厄斯金突然推开门，惊呼道。

罗尔斯面色泰然自若。「我正在向林图尔老爷禀报我如何奇妙地脱离囹圄，先生，」他说，「又说到人家如何认为，我在漫长的候审里吃的苦已够数了。这话不假。苦我吃了许多，脑子里也过了许多念头。我的见识如今是真正熟透了，法律条目也熟得吓人。可我盼着这类题目，往后再不必沾——除非出了万分紧急的情由。」罗尔斯说。他向林图尔郑重一躬，照他惯常的一板一眼、郑重其事的做派，退了出去。

===Original===

Rintoul had come to see John Erskine upon a matter of business; but they had never ceased to be friends﻿—as good friends, that is, as they ever had been. And the similarity of their situation no doubt awakened new sympathies in their minds. At least, whatever was the cause, this meeting did much to draw them together. It was now that Rintoul showed to John the real good feeling that was in him. “I have not been on your side, I confess,” he said. “I have thought Edith might do better. I don’t hide it from you. But you need not fear that I will stand in your way. I’m in the same box myself. My lord likes my affair just as little as he likes yours. But of course if she sticks fast to you, as she’ll certainly do, what can he make of it? Everything must come right in the end.”

===Chinese===

林图尔原是为一件正事来见约翰·厄斯金的；可两人从未断了朋友之交——就是说，交情同从前一样好。而处境的相似，无疑又在两颗心里唤起新的相惜。至少，无论缘故为何，这一面大大拉近了他们。正是在这时，林图尔向约翰露出了他心里真正的好意。「我一直不在你那边，这我承认，」他说。「我一向认为伊迪丝能嫁得更好。我不瞞你。可你不必怕我拦你的路。我自己也在同一条船上。老爷瞧我的事，同瞧你的事一样不顺眼。可她既然咬定了你——她一定会的——他还能怎么样呢？到头来，一切自会顺遂。」

## XLVIII / 四十八
===Original===

Thus between threats and promises, and patience and obstinacy, it came gradually to pass that Lord Lindores had to yield. He made that winter a very unhappy one to his family﻿—and it was not more agreeable to himself; for it was not long before he arrived at the conviction that he could make nothing by his opposition. In Rintoul’s case, this had been evident to him from the very first, but he had tried for some time to delude himself with the idea that Edith would and must yield to his will. The successive stages of wrath, bewildered surprise, impatient certainty, and then of a still more disagreeable conviction that whatever he might say or do he would not overcome this girl, went over him one after another, irritating and humiliating his arbitrary spirit. A father may consent to the fact that beyond a certain point he cannot coerce his full-grown son; but to be opposed and vanquished by a chit of a girl, is hard upon him. To see a soft, small creature, whom he could almost blow away, whom he could crush in his hand like a butterfly, standing up in all the force of a distinct and independent being before him, and asserting her own will and judgment against his﻿—this was almost more than he could bear. He came, however, gradually to a perception of what can and what cannot be done in the way of moral compulsion. It had succeeded with Carry, and he had not been able at first to imagine that it would not succeed equally with Edith; but gradually his mind was undeceived. He had in reality given up the contest long before he would confess to himself, and still longer before he would allow to the world that it was so. If he could do nothing else, he would at least keep his household in suspense, and make the cup as bitter as possible to them before they should be allowed to touch the sweet.

===Chinese===

就这样，在威胁与许愿、忍耐与执拗之间，事情渐渐到了林多雷斯勋爵（Lord Lindores）不得不让步的地步。那个冬天他叫一家人过得很不痛快——他自己也未见得好受；因为不久他便确信，对抗于他无利可图。林图尔那一头，他起初就看得明白；可有一阵他还想骗自己，以为伊迪丝会、也必须屈从他的意志。愤怒、错愕、不耐烦的断定，随后又是一种更不得劲的确信——无论他说什么做什么，都压不倒这个姑娘——这一层层相继碾过他，激恼着、羞辱着他那专断的心性。做父亲的尽可以承认：儿子成年之后，越过某条界线便强按不得；可是被一个黄毛丫头顶住、击败，就难受了。眼看着一个软软的小东西——他一口气几乎吹得跑、一伸手几乎捏得碎，如捏一只蝴蝶——以一个独立的、自成一体的生命的全部气力立在他面前，拿她的意志和判断对抗他的——这他几乎受不住。不过他渐渐悟出了道德强制这条路上什么行得通、什么行不通。在卡丽身上它成功过，起初他想不出为什么在伊迪丝身上不会同样成功；可他的头脑渐渐被点破。实际上，早在肯对自己承认之前——更早在肯对世人承认之前——他就放弃了这场较量。倘若别的做不成，至少他叫满宅人悬着心，在他们许尝那口甜之前，把杯子先弄到苦透。

===Original===

Lord Lindores, with all these vexations upon his head, experienced for a moment an absolute pause in his individual career and prospects. He was assailed with that disgust which is one of the curses of age and experience. Cui bono? it is the oldest of reflections and the most persistent. To what good is all the work and labour under the sun? What did it matter to him to gain an empty distinction, if his children were to melt away on all sides of him, and merge into the lower classes﻿—which was how, in a moment of natural exasperation, he represented the matter to himself. But afterwards there was a reaction, as was equally natural. He reflected that he was only fifty-five, and that what a man enjoys himself is more to him than anything his grandchildren are likely to enjoy. If he was sure of never having any grandchildren, it would still be worth his while to be Lord Dunearn in the peerage of Great Britain, and take his seat and wear his robes in Westminster. Till these glories were attained, what was he?﻿—a mere Scots lord, good for nothing. A man’s children are not the only interests he has in life; especially when they are married he can shake them off﻿—he can reenter the world without encumbrance. And Lord Lindores remembered that life and the pleasures of his rank could be enjoyed soberly with his wife at a moderate expense if the young people were all off his hand. He had been but an uncomfortable husband of late years, and yet he loved his wife as she loved him, in frequent disagreements, in occasional angers and impatiences, and much disappointment. What would become of the world if love did not manage to hold its footing through all these? The boys and girls of the high-flown kind are of opinion that love is too feeble to bear the destruction of the ideal. But that is all these young persons know. Love has the most robust vitality in the world﻿—it outlives everything. Lord Lindores was often irritated beyond description by his wife, who would not understand his ways, and was continually diverging into ridiculous bypaths of her own. And she was more disappointed in him﻿—more hurt and mortified by his shortcomings than words can say. But yet they loved each other.

===Chinese===

顶着这满头的烦恼，林多雷斯勋爵有一时在他个人的前程上陷入绝对的停顿。一种厌腻袭上他——那是年齿和阅历的咒诅之一。图什么？这是最古老、最缠人的慨叹。日头之下的一切辛劳，究竟为着什么好处？倘若儿女们四面八方从他身边消散、并进低等人家去——他在一时天然的愤懑里就是这样向自己描画这局面的——那么他挣一份空名，于他何有？可随后又有反弹，这也一样自然。他想自己才五十五岁，一个人自己享受的，比孙儿孙女可能享受的更切身。纵然拿得稳永远没有孙儿孙女，做大不列颠贵族院里的邓恩勋爵、到威斯敏斯特就席、穿起国会的袍服，于他还是值得。这些荣耀到手之前，他算什么？——一个空空洞洞的苏格兰勋爵，百无一用。儿女并非一个人在人生里仅有的挂碍；尤其他们成了亲，便可以抖落开——他可以无牵无挂地重回世界。林多雷斯勋爵又记起，待年轻人都脱了手，同妻子两个量入为出、清清爽爽地享受人生和爵位的乐趣，未尝不可。这些年来他做丈夫做得并不舒坦；可他爱他的妻子，她也爱他——在不断的龃龉、偶尔的恼怒与不耐、和深深的失望之中相爱。倘若爱情不能穿过这一切站住脚，世界还成什么世界？高调一路的少男少女们以为，理想一破，爱情便脆弱得撑不住。那只是这些年轻人懂得的全部。爱情是世上生命力最强韧的东西——它熬得过一切。林多雷斯勋爵常被妻子惹得无名火起——她不肯明白他的一套，动不动岔进她那些可笑的旁门小径。而她对他更失望——他的种种欠缺给她的伤害与羞辱，言语说不出。可他们彼此相爱。

===Original===

So much, that it gradually began to dawn upon him with a sense of solace, that when the House of Lords called him, as he hoped, he and she together, without any young people to trouble them, would yet take their pleasure together, and enjoy it and their elevated position, and be able to afford it, which was the best of all. She, at fifty, was still a handsome woman; and he had a presence which many younger men might have envied. It is doubtful whether the imagination of Lady Lindores would have been equally delighted with this dream: but it would have pleased her to know that he looked forward to it, which is next best. Animated by this thought, Lord Lindores gathered himself together and returned to public business with all his heart and soul. He took possession unhesitatingly, as has been said, of the Tinto power and influence. Torrance had opposed him in politics, and thus neutralised the advantage of a family union against which nothing in the county could stand. But now, with a sigh of satisfaction, Lord Lindores drew into his hand the influence of Tinto too.

===Chinese===

爱到这样，以至于渐渐地、带着一点安慰的意味，他开始悟到：待上议院——如他所盼——召他的时候，他同她，没有年轻人揽扰，还能一道取乐，受用这份乐趣和他们的高位，还出得起这份钱——这是顶好的一条。她五十了，仍是个好看的女人；他自有一副仪态，多少比他年轻的人都艳羡。林多雷斯夫人的想象力是否同样受用这个梦，难说；可她若知道他这样指望，也会欢喜——那是次好的一条。得了这个念头的滋养，林多雷斯勋爵重整旗鼓，全心全意回到公共事务上。他毫不迟疑地——如前所说——把廷托（Tinto）的权力和影响力攥进手里。托伦斯（Torrance）从前在政治上同他作对，抵消了两家联姻的优势——那优势原是全县无可抵御的。可如今，林多雷斯勋爵带着一声满意的叹息，把廷托的影响力也收进了掌心。

===Original===

This went on for some time with little warning of the insecurity of tenure by which he held his power. Beaufort had at last withdrawn from Dalrulzian, though it was not absolutely certain that he had left the neighbourhood. The minds of the family were, however, eased by his abandonment of the ground so far. And Lady Car lived very quietly, seldom making her appearance out of her own grounds, and never once appearing at Lindores. She would not, indeed, on any argument, return to her old home. Though she was urged by her mother and sister with many soft entreaties, Carry would never yield on this point. Her countenance seemed to blanch when it was suggested, though, she would give no reason but a tremulous oft-repeated “No, no; oh, no, no.” When she drove out, she would sometimes call at the door to fetch them, sometimes to convey them home, but they could not induce her to cross the familiar threshold. She was uneasy even in the very neighbourhood of the house, and breathed more freely when it was out of sight. This extraordinary objection to her father’s house kept her almost a prisoner in her own; for where could a widow of but a few months go, except to her parents? No other visiting was possible. She was not even, they thought, very desirous of Edith’s society, but liked to be alone, interesting herself in the alterations of furniture and new arrangements she was making; a great many of the faded grandeurs upon which Pat Torrance prided himself had already been put away. For the moment this was the only sign of feeling herself her own mistress which Lady Car displayed.

===Chinese===

这样过了一阵子，全无一点预兆显示他这份权柄的根基不稳。博福特（Beaufort）终于撤出了达尔鲁尔齐恩（Dalrulzian），虽然不能完全确定他已离开这一带。但他既放弃了那块阵地，一家人的心先松了半截。卡丽夫人过得很安静，轻易不出自家的地界，一次也没在林多雷斯露过面。任凭怎样劝说，她也不肯回娘家的老宅。母亲和妹妹百般软语央她，卡丽在这一条上始终不让。一有人提，她的脸色仿佛就发白，却什么理由也不给，只发着抖一遍遍说「不，不；哦，不，不」。她驱车出门，有时到门口接她们，有时送她们回家；可她们没法劝她跨过那道熟稔的门槛。她连那宅子的左近都不安，望不见它了才呼吸得畅快些。这层对她父亲宅子的异乎寻常的拒斥，几乎把她囚在自己家里；一个寡了才几个月的寡妇，除了父母家，还能去哪里走动？别的应酬都无从谈起。她们觉得，她甚至不很想同伊迪丝作伴，倒爱独处，专心摆弄家具的改动和她正着手的种种新布置；帕特·托伦斯引以自许的许多褪色的铺张，已经收起来了。一时之间，这是卡丽夫人表现出的唯一一点自己做主的迹象。

===Original===

Other revolutions, however, were at hand. There came a moment when it happened that one of the orders Lord Lindores had given was disobeyed, and when an explanation was asked, the answer given was that Lady Car herself had given other orders. This irritated her father greatly, and he made up his mind that the uncertainty in which things were could exist no longer﻿—that he must have an explanation with his daughter. He set out for this purpose with a little impatient determination to bring Carry to her senses. He had been tolerating much which it was ridiculous to go on tolerating. All the family had humoured her, he felt, as if she had been an inconsolable widow, brokenhearted and incapable of any exertion. At this, he could not but smile within himself as he thought of it. It was a pity, perhaps, for Torrance, poor fellow, but it could not be doubted that it was a most fortunate accident for Car. To be his wife, perhaps, had its disagreeables, but there could be no more desirable position than that of his widow; and to indulge Carry’s whims as they had all been doing, and keep every annoyance out of her way as if she had been heartbroken, was too absurd. He decided that it would be well to have a clear understanding once for all. She was left by the will in uncontrolled authority, and it was full time to show her that this did not, of course, interfere with the authority of her father, who was her natural guide and protector. “Your husband, of course, took this into consideration,” he intended to say. But it cannot be denied that he had to brace himself up for the interview with a clear sense that it might be a painful one; and that as he went along Lord Lindores did, what was a great tribute to the altered position of Carry﻿—arranged the subjects of their interview in his mind, and settled with himself what he was to say.

===Chinese===

然而别的变局已在眼前。有那么一天，林多雷斯勋爵下的某道吩咐竟没人遵从；追问缘由，回话说卡丽夫人自己另下了吩咐。这大大激恼了他，他拿定主意：这种悬而未决的局面不能再拖下去——他必须同女儿摊牌。他为此动身，带着一点不耐烦的决断，要把卡丽唤回她的理性。他容忍得够多了，再容忍下去就要闹笑话。他觉得全家都在惯她，把她当个哀恸欲绝的寡妇，心碎得什么也做不得。想到这里，他内心不能不发笑。托伦斯可怜归可怜，可这桩事故于卡丽是最走运的，这一点无可怀疑。做他的妻子，兴许有种种不快；做他的寡妇，再没有比那更可意的处境了。像他们大家这样由着卡丽的性子、替她把一切烦恼都挡开，当她当真心碎了一般，实在太荒唐。他决定，干脆来个一劳永逸的明白交涉。遗嘱把不受掣肘的权柄留给了她，那么正该叫她看看：这自然碍不着她父亲的权威——他可是她天然的监护人和保护人。「你丈夫，自然，是把这一层考虑到了的，」他预备这样说。可不能否认，他去赴这场会面前得先鼓一鼓劲，清楚这可能是场痛苦的会面；而一路上，林多雷斯勋爵做了一件对卡丽改变了的地位堪称大敬意的事——在心里把谈话的题目排了排队，拿定了要说什么。

===Original===

A great deal can happen in a neighbourhood even when it is full of gossiping society, without reaching the ears of the persons most intimately concerned, and Lord Lindores had been kept in ignorance of much which had alarmed and disquieted his wife. She was aware, but he was not, that Beaufort still lingered in the vicinity, not living indeed in one place, but making frequent expeditions from Edinburgh, or from the further north, sometimes to the little hotel at Dunearn, sometimes to other little towns in the neighbourhood, from which he could come for the day, or even for a few hours, to see Carry in her solitude. Lady Lindores had discovered this with all the pain of anxiety and wounded disapproval﻿—wounded that Carry could think it right to do what seemed to herself so little suited to the dignity and delicacy of her position: and though scarcely a word had been said between them on the subject, it had brought pain and embarrassment into their intercourse; for Carry was irritated and wounded beyond measure by the consciousness of her mother’s disapproval. She, of whom Torrance had declared in his brutal way that she was too proud to go wrong, was incapable indeed even of conceiving the possibility that “going wrong” should be in anyone’s thought of her. In her own mind, the fervour with which she had turned back to the love of her life, the eagerness with which, at the very earliest moment, she had sought his pardon, were the only compensations she could give him for the falsehood into which she had been forced and the sufferings that had been inflicted upon him. How could she pretend to build a wall of false delicacy around herself and keep him at a distance, while her heart was solely bent upon making up to him for what he had suffered, and conscious of no sentiment but an overwhelming desire for his presence and society? That she should be obliged to enjoy this society almost by stealth, and that her mother, even her mother, should object and remonstrate, gave Carry the keen and sharp offence with which a delicate mind always resents a false interpretation of its honest meaning. It seemed to her that her first duty now was to be true﻿—always true.

===Chinese===

一个地方哪怕满是长舌的交际场，也会有许多事传不进当事者的耳朵；搅扰、惊动了妻子的许多事，林多雷斯勋爵一直蒙在鼓里。她知道、他不知道的是：博福特仍在这一带盘桓——固然不在一处常住，却时时从爱丁堡（Edinburgh）、或更北边过来，有时下在邓恩（Dunearn）的小旅店，有时住左近别的小镇，从那里当天、甚至几个钟头地赶来，看望幽居中的卡丽。林多雷斯夫人发现了这一层，怀着焦灼和伤心的不以为然——伤心的是卡丽竟以为做得对，做这桩在她看来同她身份的尊严与体面这样不相称的事：两人之间在这题目上几乎没交谈过一个字，它却把痛楚和窘迫带进了她们的相处；因为母亲的不以为然，叫卡丽激愤和受伤到了无以复加。她——托伦斯曾用他那粗鲁的说法断言她太傲、不会失足的那个人——实在连「失足」二字会进任何人对她的念头这一点，都无法想象。在她自己心里，她带着怎样的一腔热回到她此生的爱情，怎样在最早的一刻急急去求他的饶恕，那是她仅能补给他的——为那场被强加于她的虚假、为他受过的苦。她的心一心只想补偿他所受的一切，除了要他在场、要他作伴的压倒的渴望之外再无别的情感，这时候叫她假装在自己四围筑一道虚假体面的墙、把他隔在远处，怎么可能？而这作伴她竟几乎得偷偷地享受；而她的母亲，连她的母亲，也反对、也进言——这给了卡丽那种尖利的刺痛：一颗细腻的心对于自己的诚实被人曲解，向来是要愤懑的。在她看来，她如今的第一桩本分就是真——永远真。

===Original===

She had been false with horrible consequences: to conceal now the eager bound of her heart towards her true lover would be a lie﻿—especially to him who had suffered, as she also had suffered, from the lies of her life. But Lord Lindores, when he made up his mind that Carry must be brought to her senses, was in no way aware how difficult the position was, and how far those senses had gone astray.

He had taken a considerable round to think over the subject, so that it was getting towards evening when he rode up the long avenue to Tinto﻿—so late that the workmen whom Carry employed in the changes she was making were leaving their work, when Lord Lindores went into the house and made his way towards Carry’s sitting-room. He sent away the butler, who, with an air of alarm and surprise, started out of the partial twilight to conduct him to his daughter. It was, he felt, something of a reproach to him that the man looked so much startled, as if his mistress’s father could be an unwelcome visitor. The room was not lighted, save by the glow of a large fire, when Lord Lindores opened the door, after a knock to which no answer was returned. There was a sound of several voices, and he was surprised to see the tall figure of a man standing against the firelight. Who was the man who was visiting Carry? It was not Rintoul, nor anyone else he knew in the neighbourhood. Nobody about was so tall, so slight, though there was something in the outline of the figure that was familiar to him. But there was an agitated conversation going on, which made the speakers scarcely distinguishable in the twilight, unconscious of the knock of the newcomer or his entrance. To his surprise it was his wife’s voice which he heard first, saying tremulously: “Mr. Beaufort, I can do nothing but return to what I said before. *Qui s’excuse s’accuse.* You may have the very best of reasons, but it is an injury to Carry that you should stay here.”

“An injury to me! How can it be an injury to me? It is my only consolation, it is the only help I have. I have told you from the first, mamma. Edward has been wronged, only not so cruelly wronged as I was myself; oh, nobody could be that! And now that we can make it up to each other﻿—and learn to forget it﻿—you would chase him away a second time﻿—for what?﻿—because of what *people*﻿—the world﻿—those who know nothing about us﻿—may say!”

===Chinese===

她曾经假过，后果可怕；如今再要遮掩她的心朝真爱那一跃，便是又一重谎——尤其是对他，这个同她一样吃过她人生里那些谎的苦的人。可林多雷斯勋爵拿定主意要唤卡丽回神时，全不知道这处境有多难，也不知道她的「神」早已走失到了什么地步。

他绕了相当一大圈把题目想透，待他骑马走上廷托那条长长的林荫道，已近黄昏——晚得卡丽雇来做改动的那批工匠正在收工。林多雷斯勋爵走进宅子，朝卡丽的起居室去。管家从半昏的暮色里惊跳出来要为他引路，被他打发走了。那人一脸的惊惶，他自觉这于他不啻一声责备——仿佛女主人的父亲竟会是不受欢迎的来客。敲了一阵门无人应，林多雷斯勋爵推门进去。屋里没点灯，只亮着一炉旺火的红光。几副人声正说着话，他惊讶地看见一道高个子男人的身影立在火光前。来探望卡丽的这人是谁？不是林图尔，也不是他在这一带认得的任何人。左近没有人这样高、这样瘦——虽然那身形的轮廓有几分眼熟。可一场激动的谈话正在进行，说话的人在暮色里几乎分辨不清，也没觉察新来者的叩门和进入。叫他吃惊的是，头一个听出的竟是他妻子林多雷斯夫人（Lady Lindores）的声音，颤颤地说：「博福特先生，我只能说回到我先前的话上。*谁辩白，谁招供*。您的理由尽可以是顶好的，可您留在这儿，于卡丽是一种伤害。」

「伤害我！怎么会伤害我？这是我唯一的安慰，我唯一的支撑。我从头一天就告诉过您了，妈妈。爱德华受了冤屈，只是没有我自家受的那样惨；哦，谁也受不到那个份上！如今我们既能彼此补偿——学着忘掉它——您却要把他第二次赶走——为什么？——就为*人家*——世人——那些对我们一无所知的人——会说的闲话！」

===Original===

Carry was standing by the mantelpiece, her tall figure in its black clinging dress scarcely distinguishable at first, but the animation with which she spoke, and the natural eloquence of her gestures, brought it out against the white marble. Then there came Beaufort’s deeper voice: “You know, Lady Lindores, I am ready to do whatever is best for her. If I can comfort her after all that has happened to her, how can I go away? I wish to do only what is best for her.”

“I beg to remark,” said Lord Lindores, coming forward, “that I knocked before coming in. This, I suppose, is why your servant looked alarmed when he admitted me. Is this gentleman, may I ask, living here?”

Carry drew back at the sound of his voice as if she had received a blow. She clung to the edge of the tall white mantelpiece, shrinking, her figure drawn together, an impersonation of terror and trouble. Beaufort started too, but slightly, and stood instinctively out of the way to make room for the newcomer. Lord Lindores went straight forward to the fire and took up his position with his back to it, with a certain straightforward ease and authority, like a man in his own house, who has no doubt of his right to do his pleasure there. But as a matter of fact, he was by no means so certain as he looked.

“We did not hear you,” said Carry, with a breathless gasp in her voice. “We were talking﻿—over points on which my mother does not agree with me.”

“I can easily imagine that,” he replied.

And then there was a dreadful pause. Lady Lindores, on the other side of the fire, did not move or speak. It was the crisis of Carry’s fate, and except in defence or help of her child, the mother vowed to herself that she would take no part. It was hard, but it was best for Carry. Whatever was going to happen to her, she must decide for herself now.

“I asked,” said Lord Lindores in that calm, clear, collected voice, which was so strange a contrast to the agitation of the others, “whether this gentleman is living here? If so, it is very inappropriate and unsuitable. Your mother would prefer, I am sure, if Mr. Beaufort is here about any business, to offer him a bed at Lindores.”

There was a universal holding of the breath at this extraordinary proposition. Had he burst into all the violence of passion, they would have been prepared, but not for this politeness and calm.

===Chinese===

卡丽立在壁炉台旁，她那高挑的身形裹在黑贴身的衣裙里，起初几乎看不出来；可她说话时的神采、她手势里天生的雄辩，把它衬上了白色的大理石。随后响起博福特低沉些的嗓音：「您知道的，林多雷斯夫人，凡于她顶好的事我都准备去做。发生了这一切之后，我若能安慰她，我怎么能走？我只想做于她顶好的事。」

「请容我说一句，」林多雷斯勋爵上前道，「我进来之前敲过门。想来这就是贵仆开门时一脸惊惶的缘故了。这位绅士，我可否问一问，是住在此地？」

听见他的声音，卡丽像挨了一击似的缩了回去。她攀住那高高的白色壁炉台的边，瑟缩着，身子收作一团，一副惊惶与痛苦的化身。博福特也一惊，却很轻微，随即本能地侧身让开，给新来者腾出地方。林多雷斯勋爵径直走到炉前，背炉而立，带着某种直截了当的从容与威严，像在自己家里的男人，对自己在那里为所欲为的权利毫不怀疑。可事实上，他远不像看上去那样有把握。

「我们没听见，」卡丽说，声音里带着透不过气的喘。「我们在谈——谈些母亲同我意见不合的事。」

「这我容易想见，」他答道。

随后是一阵可怕的静默。林多雷斯夫人在炉火另一侧，一动不动，一言不发。这是卡丽命运的关头；这位母亲对自己立了誓：除了护卫和搭救她的孩子，她一概不插手。难，可于卡丽顶好。无论等着她的是什么，如今她必须自己拿主意。

「我问的是，」林多雷斯勋爵用那副平静、清明、镇定的声调说——同其余人的激动对比得那样古怪——「这位绅士是不是住在此地？若是，那就非常失当、非常不合式。博福特先生若为此地什么事而来，我相信您母亲会宁愿请他到林多雷斯去住一晚的。」

这句离奇的话叫在场的人一齐屏住了呼吸。他若是破门而入、大发雷霆，他们倒有防备；却没有防备这份客气与平静。

===Original===

“I am not living here, Lord Lindores,” said Beaufort, with some confusion. “I am on my way from the North. I could not resist the temptation of staying for an hour or two on my way to inquire﻿—”

“That was very kind,” he said; “and kindness which interferes with personal comfort is very rare. If you are going to Edinburgh, you must remember you have two ferries to cross.”

“Probably,” Beaufort cried, faltering a little, “I shall stay all night in Dunearn. Lady Caroline﻿—had some commissions for me.”

“You had much better come to Lindores. Commissions, Carry! I suppose Mr. Beaufort is acting as a sort of agent for you in your new arrangements. Is it bric-a-brac? You young men are all learned in that.”

Nobody made any reply, but the very air seemed to tingle with the extraordinary tumult of feeling. To accept Beaufort as an ordinary caller, and to invite him to Lindores, was a masterstroke. But the two people between whom he stood were so surcharged with passionate feeling, that any touch must produce an explosion of one sort or another. This touch was given inadvertently by Lady Lindores, who﻿—terribly bewildered by the course that things were taking, but feeling that if Beaufort could be induced to go to Lindores, it would cut the thread better than any other expedient﻿—rose softly out of the twilight, and coming forward to him, laid her hand upon his arm: “Yes, yes, that is much the best. Come to Lindores,” she said.

At which Carry lost the control of herself which people in their ordinary senses have. Between panic and passion she was beside herself. Fear has a wild temerity which goes far beyond courage;﻿—her tall straight figure seemed to fling suddenly out of the shade, and launch itself upon this milder group. She put Lady Lindores away with a vehement gesture.

“Mother,” she cried, “do not you meddle. Edward! do not go, do not go; it is a trap, it is a snare. If you go it will all be over, all over!” Her voice rose almost to a scream. She had reached the point at which reason has no longer any hold, and all the reticence and modesty of nature yields to the wild excitement of terror. She was trembling all over, yet capable of any supreme effort of desperation﻿—ready to defend to the last, against the same powers that had crushed her before, her last hope.

===Chinese===

「我没有住在这儿，林多雷斯勋爵，」博福特带着几分窘说。「我正从北边过来。路过时忍不住要停留一两个钟头，来问一问——」

「真是盛情，」他说；「损害自身安适的盛情，尤其难得。您若是去爱丁堡，记住路上要过两道渡口。」

「多半，」博福特喊道，有点结巴，「我要在邓恩过夜。卡罗琳夫人——托我办几件事。」

「那还不如到林多雷斯来住。办事！卡丽！想必博福特先生是替你的新布置做一类经纪人吧。是古董摆件？你们年轻人个个都精通此道。」

没有人答话，可空气本身仿佛都因那阵异样的情感激荡而刺痛起来。把博福特当寻常访客接纳、又请他去林多雷斯住，是一记高手。可他居中插着的这两个人，情感充得太满，随便一触都要引发这样或那样一场爆发。这一触是不小心由林多雷斯夫人给出的——事情这样发展，她惶恐极了；可她觉得，若能劝得博福特去林多雷斯，比任何别的法子都更能一刀剪断这根线——于是她从暮色里悄然起身，走向他，把手搭上他的胳膊：「是，是，那样顶好。来林多雷斯吧，」她说。

这一下，卡丽失去了神志清明的人所有的自制。恐慌与激情交攻，她疯了。恐惧自有一种狂胆，远远超过勇气；——她那高挑笔直的身影仿佛突然从暗影里掷出，扑向这群温和的人。她一个猛烈的姿势把林多雷斯夫人拨开。

「妈妈，」她喊道，「你别掺和。爱德华！别去，别去；那是个圈套，是个罗网。你一去就全完了，全完了！」她的声音几乎升成尖叫。她已到了理性再握不住的那一点，天性全部的含蓄与羞怯都让位于恐怖的狂乱。她浑身发抖，却还使得出孤注一掷的任何全力——准备好最后一搏，对抗那些从前碾碎过她的同一些力量，守住她最后的希望。

===Original===

“Carry,” said Lord Lindores﻿—he kept up, at incalculable cost to himself, his tone of conciliation﻿—“I do not understand what you fear. Is it I that am to lay traps or snares? I forgive you, my poor child; but this is a strange way to talk to Mr. Beaufort﻿—he cannot stay here﻿—”

“I have no intention of staying here, Lord Lindores,” said Beaufort hastily. “You may be sure I will not expose her to any comment.”

“I am very sure, nevertheless, that you are doing so,” said Lord Lindores.

The contrast of this brief dialogue with Carry’s impassioned tones was extraordinary. She felt it through the haze of excitement that surrounded her, though her intelligence of all outside matters was blurred by the wild strain of her own feelings, which would have utterance. “Father,” she said hoarsely, putting her hand on his arm, “go away from us﻿—do not interfere. You know what you made of me when I was in your hands. Oh, let us alone now! I am not a girl﻿—I am a woman. I am the same as you, knowing good and evil. Oh,” she said suddenly, “if you want to keep any respect for me, go away, go away, for I don’t know what I am saying. My head is turning round. Mother﻿—Edward; don’t you see that I am losing my reason? Oh, don’t let him interfere﻿—let him go away.” Lady Lindores caught her daughter in her arms, in a trembling effort to control and calm her. “Carry, my dearest! you will be sorry afterwards﻿—”

“Oh yes, I shall be sorry,” cried poor Lady Car, drawing herself out of her mother’s hold﻿—“sorry to have been unkind, sorry to have betrayed myself; but I must, I must. I cannot hold my peace. Oh, father, let me alone! What good will that do you to make me wretched? What good has it done you? Nothing, nothing! I might have been poor and happy, instead of all I have come through; and what difference would it have made to you? You have killed me once; but oh, think how cruel, how tyrannous, if you tried to kill me again! And you see nobody speaks for me; I am alone to defend myself. Father, you shall not interfere again.”

===Chinese===

「卡丽，」林多雷斯勋爵说——他维持着劝抚的声调，于自己代价难以估量——「我不明白你怕什么。设陷阱、布罗网的，难道是我？我饶恕你，我可怜的孩子；可这样同博福特先生说话，未免离奇——他不能住在这里——」

「我没有要住在这里的意思，林多雷斯勋爵，」博福特急忙说。「您尽可放心，我不会叫她受一句闲话。」

「尽管如此，我确信你正在这样做，」林多雷斯勋爵说。

这一段短短的对白，同卡丽激越的声调对比得太悬殊了。隔着裹住她的那层迷雾她也感觉到了，虽然她对外界一切的知解，都被自家那非要出口不可的狂烈情感模糊了。「父亲，」她哑着嗓子说，一只手按上他的胳膊，「离开我们——别插手。您把我攥在手里时，把我做成了什么样，您知道。哦，如今放过我们吧！我不是姑娘了——我是个妇人。我同您一样，识得善与恶。哦，」她忽然说，「您若还想对我存几分敬意，就走吧，走吧，因为我不知道自己在说什么了。我的头在转。妈妈——爱德华；你们看不出我正在失掉理性吗？哦，别让他插手——让他走。」林多雷斯夫人一把搂住女儿，颤着劲要按住她、平息她。「卡丽，我最亲爱的！过后你会后悔的——」

「哦是，我会后悔，」可怜的卡丽夫人喊道，从母亲怀里挣出来——「后悔方才的狠，后悔泄露了自己；可我必须，我必须。我缄不了口。哦，父亲，放过我！叫我痛苦，于您有什么好处？从前又得了什么好处？什么也没有，什么也没有！我本可以又穷又快活，而不是经了这一切；那于您又有什么两样？您已经杀过我一次了；哦，想想吧，多狠，多专横，您若想再杀我一次！您看，没有一个人替我说话；我孤身一个，自家护自家。父亲，您不许再插手。」

===Original===

She had resumed her hold on his arm, grasping it half to support herself, half to enforce what she was saying. He now put his hand upon hers and detached it gently, still keeping down his anger, retaining his tone of calm. “My poor child, you are overdone; let your mother take care of you,” he said compassionately. “Mr. Beaufort, we are both out of place here at this moment. Lady Caroline has had a great deal to try her; we had better leave her with her mother.” Nobody could be more reasonable, more temperate. His compassionate voice and gentle action, and the way in which he seemed about to sweep away with him the somewhat irresolute figure of the man who had no right to be there, filled Carry with a wild pang. It seemed to her that, notwithstanding all her protest and passion, he was about to be victorious once more, and to rob her of all life and hope again. She stretched out her arms wildly, with a cry of anguish: “Edward, are you going to forsake me too?”

Edward Beaufort was very pertinacious in his love, very faithful, poetically tender and true, but he was not strong in an emergency, and the calmness and friendliness of Lord Lindores’ address deceived him. He cried “Never!” with the warmest devotion: but then he changed his tone a little: “Lord Lindores is perhaps right﻿—for the moment. I must not﻿—bring ill-natured remark﻿—”

Lady Car burst into a little wild laugh. “You have no courage﻿—you either,” she said, “even you. It is only I, a poor coward, that am not afraid. It is not natural to me, everybody knows; but when a soul is in despair﻿—Then just see how bold I am,” she cried suddenly, “father and mother! If there is any holding back, it is his, not mine. I have been ready﻿—ready from the first, as I am now. I care nothing about remark, or what anybody says. I will hear no reason; I will have no interference. Do you hear me, all? Do you hear what I say?”

“I hear﻿—what I am very sorry to hear, Carry﻿—what you cannot mean. Mr. Beaufort is too much a gentleman to take advantage of this wild talk, which is mere excitement and overstrained feeling.”

===Chinese===

她重新抓住他的胳膊，一半撑住自己，一半加重她的话。他把手覆在她手上，轻轻掰开，仍压着怒气，维持着平静的声调。「我可怜的孩子，你是撑过头了；让你母亲照看你吧，」他怜惜地说。「博福特先生，此刻我们两个都待得不是地方。卡罗琳夫人受的磨折太多了；咱们还是把她留给她母亲吧。」再没有比这更讲理、更克制的了。他那怜惜的声音、温和的举止，还有他那种眼看要连那个无权在此的人那副迟疑的身影一并卷走带去的架势，叫卡丽一阵狂痛。在她看来，任凭她怎样抗议、怎样激愤，他又要得胜了，又要再一次夺去她全部的生命和希望。她狂乱地张开双臂，一声哀号：「爱德华，你也要丢下我吗？」

爱德华·博福特在他的爱情里极坚忍、极忠贞，有诗意的温存和真挚；可临到急难他不算刚强，林多雷斯勋爵言辞的平静与友好骗过了他。他怀着最热的赤诚喊了声「决不！」；可随即声调又变了一变：「林多雷斯勋爵兴许说得对——暂时如此。我不能——招来恶意的闲话——」

卡丽夫人迸出一声狂乱的小笑。「你们没有胆量——你也没有，」她说，「连你也没有。只有我一个可怜的懦夫，天不怕地不怕。这不合我的本性，谁都知道；可一个灵魂到了绝望——那就看看我多大胆，」她忽然喊道，「爸爸，妈妈！要是有谁退缩，那是他，不是我。我从头一天起就准备好了——如今还是。闲话也罢，人家怎么说也罢，我一概不管。我什么道理也不要听；谁也不许插手。你们听见没有，全体？听见我说的话没有？」

「我听见了——听得很痛心，卡丽——听见了你决不会当真的话。博福特先生是十足的绅士，不会利用这一番疯话——那不过是激动和过火的情感。」

===Original===

She laughed again, that laugh, which is no laugh, but an expression of all that is inarticulate in the highest excitement. “I am ready﻿—to fulfil our old engagement, our old, old, broken engagement, that we made before God and heaven. I have been like Dante,” she said; “I have lost my way, and made that dreadful round before I could find it, through hell and purgatory; yes, that is it﻿—through hell﻿—And now, whenever Edward pleases. It is not I that am holding back. Yes, go, go!” she said; “oh, though I love you, you are not like me, you have not suffered like me! go﻿—but don’t go with my father. He will find some way of putting everything wrong again.”

The two gentlemen walked solemnly, one behind the other, to the door: on the threshold Lord Lindores paused. “I don’t suppose you will suspect me of any designs upon your life,” he said, with a bitter smile, “if I repeat that you will be welcome at Lindores.”

“I had made all my arrangements,” said Beaufort, with some confusion, “to stay at Dunearn.”

Lord Lindores paused for a moment before mounting his horse. “All that she has been saying is folly,” he said; “you may be certain that it will not be permitted﻿—”

“Who is to stop it? I don’t think, if we are agreed, anyone has the power.”

“It will not be permitted. It would be disgraceful to you. It would be a step that no gentleman could take. A foolish young woman, hysterical with excitement and exhaustion and grief﻿—”

“Lord Lindores, you forget what that young woman has been to me﻿—ever since I have known her. I have never wavered﻿—”

===Chinese===

她又笑了——那种不算笑的笑，是极度激动中一切说不出的东西的表露。「我准备好了——履行我们旧日的婚约，我们那旧的、旧的、破了的婚约，在上帝和上天面前立下的。我一直像但丁，」她说；「我迷了路，绕了那可怕的一整圈才找回来——穿过地狱和炼狱；是，正是这样——穿过地狱——如今，只等爱德华愿意。退缩的不是我。是，去吧，去吧！」她说；「哦，我虽然爱你，你可不像我，你没受过我这样的苦！去吧——可别跟我父亲一道走。他会想法子把一切又弄糟的。」

两位绅士一前一后，郑重地走到门口：在门槛上，林多雷斯勋爵停了停。「想必你不会疑心我对你的性命有什么图谋，」他带着苦笑说，「所以我再说一遍：林多雷斯欢迎你。」

「我原已把一切都安排好了，」博福特有些窘地说，「在邓恩住。」

上马之前，林多雷斯勋爵又顿了一顿。「她方才说的那些全是昏话，」他说；「你可以拿得稳，那是不会获准的——」

「谁来拦？只要我们两厢情愿，我想谁也没有这个权力。」

「不会获准的。那于你是耻辱。那是一步没有绅士肯迈的步子。一个愚蠢的年轻女人，激动、衰竭、悲伤得歇斯底里——」

「林多雷斯勋爵，您忘了那个年轻女人于我是什么——打我认得她起。我从没有动摇过——」

===Original===

“Then you have committed a sin,” the Earl said. He stood there discomfited, in the darkness of the night, scarcely remembering the servants, who were within hearing﻿—not knowing what further step to take. He raised his foot to put it in the stirrup, then turned back again. “If you will not come with me﻿—where we could talk this out at our leisure﻿—at least you will go away from here,” he said. Beaufort did not reply in words, but hastened away, disappearing in the gloom of the avenue. Lord Lindores mounted his horse, and followed slowly, in a tumult of thought. He had not been prepared for it﻿—he was unable now to realise the power of wild and impassioned resistance which was in Carry. He was giddy with astonishment, as if his horse or his dog had turned round upon him and defied him. But he tried to shake off the impression as he got further from Tinto. It was impossible; it was a mere bravado. She would no more hold to it than﻿—And since there was delicacy, decorum, propriety﻿—every reason that could be thought of, on the other side﻿—no, no! He would forgive poor Carry’s passion, for she could no more hold to it﻿—Even her mother, who had been so difficult to manage before, her mother would fully support him now. He tried to console himself with these thoughts; but yet Lord Lindores rode home a broken man.

===Chinese===

「那你就犯下了罪，」伯爵说。他站在那里，狼狈不堪，处在夜的黑暗里，连听得见声息的仆人们都忘了——不知道下一步该怎么走。他抬脚要踏进马镫，又转回身。「你若不肯随我去——去个可以从容把话谈透的地方——至少你总肯离开这里吧，」他说。博福特没有回话，匆匆走了，消失在林荫道的幽暗里。林多雷斯勋爵上了马，缓缓跟在后面，思绪翻腾。他没有防备——此刻也无法估量卡丽身上那股狂野而热烈的反抗之力。他晕眩于惊愕，仿佛他的马、他的狗掉过头来顶撞了他。可离廷托愈远，他愈想把这印象甩掉。不可能的；那不过是一时逞凶。她决不会真照办，正如——何况体面、规矩、礼法——能想得到的理由全在另一边——不，不！他会饶恕可怜的卡丽的激愤，因为她决不会真照办——就连她母亲，先前那样难以对付的母亲，如今也会全力支持他的。他拿这些念头宽解自己；可林多雷斯勋爵骑马到家时，已是一个被击垮的人。

===Original===

Lady Lindores sat and cried by the fire, while Carry swept about the room in her passion, crossing and recrossing the firelight. The servants at Tinto were more judicious than those at Lindores. They were accustomed to scenes in the drawing-room, and to know that it was indiscreet to carry lights thither until they were called for. In the late Tinto’s time the lamps, when they were carried in abruptly, had lit up many an episode of trouble﻿—the fierce redness of the master’s countenance, the redness so different of his wife’s eyes. So that no one interrupted the lingering hour of twilight. Lady Lindores sat like any of the poor women in the cottages, unable to stand against the passion of her child. How familiar is the scene﻿—the mother crying by the fireside, descended from her dignity and power to sway (if she ever possessed any), to sheer helplessness and pathetic spectatorship, unable, with all the experience and gathered wisdom of her years, to suggest anything or do anything for the headstrong life and passion of the other woman, who could learn only by experience as her mother did before her. Carry paced up and down the room from end to end; even the shadowy lines of her figure, even her step, revealed the commotion of her soul: when she came full into the firelight she stood still for a moment, her hands clasped, her head thrown back, confronting the dim image of herself in the great mirror against a ruddy background of gloom. And Carry in her passion was not without enlightenment too.

“No,” she said passionately, “no, no. Do you know why I am so determined? It is because I am frightened to death. Oh, don’t take an advantage of what I am saying to you. How do I know what my father might do this time? No, no. I must keep out of his hands. I will rather die.”

“Carry, I will not interfere. What can I do between you? But these are not all conventionalities, as you think﻿—there is more in them.”

“There is this in them,” she said, with a strange pathetic smile, “that Edward thinks so too. He is not ready like me to throw away everything. He might be persuaded, perhaps, if my father put forth all his powers, to abandon me, to think it was for my interest﻿—”

“Carry, I do not wish to support you in your wild projects: but I think you are doing Edward injustice.”

===Chinese===

林多雷斯夫人坐在炉边哭，卡丽则在她的激愤里横扫过房间，来回穿过火光。廷托的仆人比林多雷斯的家仆更有分寸。他们见惯了客厅里的场面，知道灯不叫拿就往里拿是不明智的。在已故的廷托手里，灯猛地端进去时，照亮过多少回风波——主人那张暴红的脸，他太太那双红得另一样的眼睛。所以没有人来搅扰这段拖延的黄昏。林多雷斯夫人坐在那里，同茅舍里的穷女人一样，敌不过她的孩子的激愤。这场景何其熟悉——做母亲的坐在炉边哭，从她的尊严和威权（倘若她有过的话）跌落到全然的无助和可怜的旁观，纵有一生的阅历和积攒的智慧，却对另一个女人的执拗的生命和激愤提不出一句、做不出一事——那另一个女人只能像她母亲当年一样，从阅历里学。卡丽从屋子这头踱到那头；连她身影的暗线、连她的脚步，都透出她灵魂的激荡：待她整个走进火光，她便立定片刻，双手交握，头向后仰，迎着大镜中那以红暗为背景的自己的朦胧映像。激愤中的卡丽也并非没有清明。

「不，」她激烈地说，「不，不。你知道我为什么这样拿得死？因为我怕得要死。哦，别拿我这句话来占便宜。我怎么知道我父亲这一回会做出什么？不，不。我必须逃出他的手心。我宁可死。」

「卡丽，我不插手。你们两个中间，我能做什么？可这些并不全是你以为的俗套虚文——里头另有分量。」

「里头的分量是，」她说，带着一种古怪而凄婉的笑，「爱德华也这样想。他不像我，还没到抛开一切的地步。倘若我父亲使出全部的手段，他说不定会被劝动，丢下我，当作是为我好——」

「卡丽，我不想助长你那些疯狂的打算：可我看你冤枉了爱德华。」

===Original===

“Thank you, mother dear; your voice is so sweet,” she said, with a sudden softening, “why should you cry? It is all a black sea round about me on every side. I have only one thing to cling to, only one thing, and how can I tell? perhaps that may fail me too. But you have nothing to cry for. Your way is all clear and straight before you till it ends in heaven. Let them talk as they like, there must be heaven for you. You will sit there and wait and watch to see all the broken boats come home﻿—some bottom upwards, and every one drowned; some lashed to one miserable bit of a mast﻿—like me.”

“Carry,” said Lady Lindores, “if that is the case﻿—if you do not feel sure﻿—why, in spite of everything, father and mother, and modesty and reverence, and all that is most necessary to life, your own good name, and perhaps the future welfare of your children﻿—why will you cling to Edward Beaufort? You wronged him perhaps, but he did nothing to stop it. There were things he might have done﻿—he ought to have been ready to claim you before﻿—to oppose your﻿—”

Carry threw herself at her mother’s feet, and laid her trembling hand upon her lips. “Not a word, not a word,” she cried. “Do you think he would wrong my children? Oh no, no! that is impossible. His fault, it is to be too good. And if he did nothing, what could he do? He has never had the ground to stand on, nor opportunity, nor time. Thank God! they will be his now; he will prove what is in him now.”

===Chinese===

「谢谢您，亲爱的妈妈；您的声音这样甜，」她忽然软下来说，「您哭什么呢？我的四面八方都是一片黑海。我只有一样东西抓着，只有一样，可谁知道呢？说不定连它也要叫我落空。可您没有可哭的。您的路又直又清，一直通到天堂。随他们怎么说，天堂于您总是有的。您要坐在那里，等着、望着，看一条条破船回家——有的底朝天，一船人全淹了；有的拴在一根可怜的小桅杆上——像我。」

「卡丽，」林多雷斯夫人说，「倘若事情真是这样——倘若你没有把握——那么，为什么，不顾一切——不顾父母，不顾廉耻与敬畏，不顾一切立身的必需、你自己的清名，也许还有你孩子们日后的福祉——为什么还要抓住爱德华·博福特不放？你也许亏负过他，可他当初并没有出力拦阻。他原有些事可做——他早该备好来认领你——来挡下你的——」

卡丽扑到母亲脚边，把一只发抖的手掩上她的嘴唇。「一个字也别说了，一个字也别说，」她喊道。「您想他会亏待我的孩子？哦不，不！那不可能。他的毛病，是太好。而他当初什么也没做，他能做什么呢？他从来没有立足的地，没有机会，没有工夫。感谢上帝！如今这些都要归他了；他就要显出他的本色了。」

===Original===

Which was it that in her heart she believed? But Lady Lindores could not tell. Carry, when she calmed down, sat at her mother’s feet in the firelight, and clasped her close, and poured out her heart, no longer in fiery opposition and passion, but with a sudden change and softening, in all the pathos of trouble past and hope returned. They cried together, and talked and kissed each other, once more mother and child, admitting no other thought. This sudden change went to the heart of Lady Lindores. Her daughter’s head upon her bosom, her arm holding her close, what could she do but kiss her and console her, and forget everything in sympathy. But as she drove home in the dark other fears came in. Only one thing to cling to﻿—and perhaps that might fail her﻿—“one miserable bit of a mast.” What did she mean? What did Carry believe? that her old love would renew for her all the happiness of life, as she had been saying, whispering with her cheek close to her mother’s﻿—that the one dream of humanity, the romance which is never worn out and never departs, was now to be fulfilled for her?﻿—or that, even into this dream, the canker had entered, the sense that happiness was not and never could be?

===Chinese===

她心里信的究竟是哪一样？林多雷斯夫人说不上。卡丽平静下来之后，坐在炉边的母亲脚畔，紧紧偎着她，倾吐她的心——不再是烈焰腾腾的对抗和激愤，而是陡然一变、一片柔顺，怀着苦难过后的全部凄婉和回转的希望。她们一同哭泣，又谈又吻，重又只剩母女两个，不容第三种念头。这骤变直透林多雷斯夫人的心。女儿的头偎在她胸前，她的手臂紧紧搂着她——她还能怎样，只有吻她、安慰她，在同情里忘掉一切。可当她摸黑驱车回家，别的恐惧又来了。只有一样东西抓着——说不定连它也要落空——「一根可怜的小桅杆」。她是什么意思？卡丽信的是什么？是信她的旧爱会替她赎回人生全部的幸福，如她方才贴着母亲的脸颊絮絮说的那样——信人性那一场梦、那永不磨灭、永不褪色的浪漫，如今要在她身上应验？——还是信，连这场梦里也生了蛀虫，生了那种幸福感不存在、也永不会存在的知觉？

## XLIX / 四十九
===Original===

When a pair of lovers are finally delivered from all those terrible obstacles that fret the current of true love, and are at last married and settled, what more is there to be said about them? One phase of life is happily terminated﻿—the chapter which human instinct has chosen as the subject of romance, the one in which all classes are interested﻿—those to whom it is still in the future, with all the happy interest of happiness to come﻿—those to whom it is in the past, with perhaps a sigh, perhaps a smile of compassion, a softening recollection, even when their hopes have not been fulfilled, of what was and what might have been. The happinesses and the miseries of that early struggle, how they dwindle in importance as we get older﻿—how little we think now of the crisis which seemed final then﻿—things for which heaven and earth stood still; yet there will never come a time in which human interest will fall away from the perennial story, continually going on, ever changing, yet ever the same.

===Chinese===

当一对恋人终于摆脱了那一切磨折真爱之流的可怕障碍，终成眷属、安顿下来，关于他们还有什么可说的呢？生命的一个阶段圆满收束——这一章，人类的天性选它作了传奇的题目，各阶层人人关切的一章——对那些它尚在前头的人，怀着幸福将至的全部欢然兴味——对那些它已在身后的人，或许一声叹息，或许一丝怜惜的微笑，一段心软的追忆，纵然自己的希望不曾实现，追忆那曾经有过的、和本来或许会有的。早年那场挣扎里的甘甜与苦楚，随着年岁增长，分量消退得多么快——当年仿佛是最后审判的危机，如今想也不想——那种天地为之停摆的大事；然而人心对这桩常青故事的兴味，永远不会冷淡——它不断上演，变化不息，却又永远如一。

===Original===

Before proceeding to the knotting up of other threads, we must first recount here what happened to Lord Millefleurs. He did not take any immediate steps in respect to Miss Sallie Field. They corresponded largely and fully at all times, and he told her of the little incident respecting Edith Lindores in full confidence of her sympathy and approval. Perhaps he gave the episode a turn of a slightly modified kind, representing that his proposal was rather a matter of politeness than of passion, and that it was a relief to both parties when it was discovered that Edith, as well as himself, considered fraternal much better than matrimonial relations. Miss Sallie’s reply to this was very uncompromising. She said: “I think you have behaved like a couple of fools. You ought to have married. You can tell her from me that she would have found you very nice, though your height may leave something to be desired. I don’t myself care for girls﻿—they are generally stupid; but it would have been exceedingly suitable, and pleased your parents﻿—a duty which I wish I saw you more concerned about.” Lord Millefleurs, in his reply, acknowledged the weight and sense “as always” of his correspondent’s opinion. “I told dear Edith at once what you said; but it did not perhaps make so much impression on her as it would otherwise have done, since she has got engaged to John Erskine, a country gentleman in the neighbourhood, which does not please her parents half so well as a certain other union would have done. Pleasing one’s parents after all, though it is a duty, is not paramount to all other considerations. Besides, I have never thought it was a commandment to which great attention was paid *chez nous*.” Miss Field’s reply was still more succinct and decided: “I don’t know what you mean by *chez nous*. I hate French phrases when simple American will do as well. If you think we don’t love our fathers and mothers, it just shows how far popular fallacy can go, and how easily you bigoted Englishmen are taken in. Who was it that first opened your eyes to the necessity of considering your mother’s feelings?” Peace was established after this, but on the whole Lord Millefleurs decided to await the progress of circumstances, and not startle and horrify those parents whom Miss Sallie was so urgent he should please.

===Chinese===

在续结其余线头之前，这里必须先讲讲米勒弗勒勋爵的下场。他对萨莉·菲尔德小姐并没有立即采取任何步骤。两人一向书信频繁而详尽，他把伊迪丝·林多雷斯那段小插曲原原本本告诉了她，满心以为会换来她的同情和赞许。也许他把这段公案的说法稍稍改了一改，说他的求婚冋宁说是一桩礼貌，而非一场热恋，又说到后来双方都发现，伊迪丝同他一样，认为兄妹之交远胜于夫妻之好，两人都如释重负。萨莉小姐对此的答复毫不通融。她写道：「我看你们俩的行径像一对傻子。你们本该结婚的。你可以替我转告她，她会发现你这人很不错，虽然你的个子或许差强人意。我本人不喜欢姑娘们——她们多半愚蠢；可这门亲本会再合适不过，又讨你父母欢喜——这份本分，我但愿看你多上点心。」米勒弗勒勋爵回信承认，对方的意见「一如既往」既有分量又有道理。「您说的话，我立刻转告了亲爱的伊迪丝；只是它于她的效力，也许不及平常会有的那般大，因为她已同约翰·厄斯金订了婚——本地的一位乡绅；这门亲事讨她父母欢喜的程度，远不及本来可能的那另一门。说到底，讨父母欢喜虽是本分，却压不过其余一切的考虑。再说，我从没觉得在咱们家（chez nous），这是一条受多大重视的诫命。」菲尔德小姐的回信愈发简短决绝：「我不知道你的咱们家是什么意思。好好的美国话能说清的事，我恨法国腔。你要是以为我们不爱国亲娘亲，那正好显出流行的谬见能走多远，显出你们这些心胸狭隘的英国人多么容易上当。当初是谁头一个点醒你，叫你想到该顾念你母亲的感受的？」此后太平无事，可总的说来，米勒弗勒勋爵决定静观事态，暂不去惊吓、震骇那对父母——萨莉小姐那么急切地要他讨好的那对。

===Original===

Some time after she informed him that she was coming to Europe in charge of a beautiful young niece, who would have a large fortune. “Money makes a great deal of difference in the way in which dukes and duchesses consider matters,” she wrote, enigmatically, “and so far as I can make out from your papers and novels (if there is any faith to be put in them), American girls are the fashion.” Lord Millefleurs informed his mother of this approaching arrival, and with some difficulty procured from her an invitation to Ess Castle for his Transatlantic friends. “I wish there was not that girl though,” her Grace said; but Lady Reseda, for her part, was delighted. “She will go to Paris first and bring the very newest fashions,” that young lady cried. The ducal mansion was a little excited by the anticipation. They looked for a lovely creature dressed to just a little more than perfection, who would come to breakfast in a diamond necklace, and amuse them more than anybody had amused them in the memory of man. And they were not disappointed in this hope. Miss Nellie F. Field was a charming little creature, and her “things” were divine. Lady Reseda thought her very like Daisy Miller; and the Duchess allowed, with a sigh, that American girls were the fashion, and that if Millefleurs *would* have something out of the way﻿—.

===Chinese===

过了一阵，她来信告知，她要带一位貌美的年轻侄女前来欧洲，那侄女将有一大笔财产。「钱这个东西，能让公爵和公爵夫人们考虑问题的方式大不相同，」她写得云山雾罩，「再说，照我从你们的报纸和小说里看出来的（倘若那些东西还信得过），美国姑娘正时兴。」米勒弗勒勋爵把这桩将至的来访禀明了母亲，又颇费了些周章，才从她那里为他的大西洋彼岸的朋友们讨得一张艾斯城堡的请帖。「只可惜带着那么个丫头。」公爵夫人说；雷塞达小姐倒是欢喜。「她要先去巴黎，把顶时新的时式带来。」那位小姐喊道。公爵府被这份期盼微微激动了。他们等着一位妆扮得比十全十美还要多出一分的可人儿，会戴着钻石项链下来吃早饭，逗他们开怀，开他们记忆里谁也不曾给过的怀。而这指望竟没落空。莉莉·F.·菲尔德小姐是个娇小迷人的尤物，她的「行头」妙极了。雷塞达小姐觉得她活脱是黛西·米勒；公爵夫人也叹着气承认，美国姑娘正时兴，倘若米勒弗勒偏要出格一点的——

===Original===

But in the meanwhile Millefleurs left this lovely little impersonation of Freedom to his mother and sister, and walked about with her aunt. Miss Sallie was about eight or nine and thirty, an age at which women have not ceased to be pleasant﻿—when they choose﻿—to the eye as well as to the heart. But the uncompromising character of her advice was nothing to that of her toilette and appearance. She wore short skirts in which she could move about freely when everybody else had them long. She wore a bonnet when everybody else had a hat. Her hair was thin, but she was scrupulous never to add a tress, or even a cushion. She was not exactly plain, for her features were good, and her eyes full of intelligence; but as for complexion, she had none, and no figure to speak of. She assumed the entire spiritual charge of Millefleurs from the moment they met, and he was never absent from her side a moment longer than he could help. It amused the family beyond measure, at first almost more than Nellie. But by and by the smile began to be forced, and confusion to take the part of hilarity. It was Miss Sallie Field herself at last who took the bull by the horns, if that is not too profane a simile. She took the Duke apart one fine evening, when the whole party had strolled out upon the lawn after dinner﻿—“Your son,” she said, “is tormenting me to marry him,” and she fixed upon the Duke her intelligent eyes. His Grace was confounded, as may be supposed. He stood aghast at this middle-aged woman with her Transatlantic accent and air. He did not want to be uncivil. “You!” he said, in consternation, then blushed for his bad manners, and added, suavely, “I beg you a thousand pardons﻿—you mean﻿—your niece.” That of itself would be bad enough. “No,” said Miss Sallie, with an air of regret, “it does not concern Nellie. I have told him that would be more reasonable. Nellie is very pretty, and has a quantity of money; but he doesn’t seem to see it. Perhaps you don’t know that this was what he wanted when I sent him home to his mother? I thought he would have got over it when he came home. I consider him quite unsuitable for me, but I am a little uneasy about the moral consequences. I am thirty-eight, and I have a moderate competency, not a fortune, like Nellie. I thought it better to talk it over with you before it went any further,” Miss Sallie said.

与此同时，米勒弗勒把这位自由的可人化身留给母亲和妹妹，自己陪着她的姑母四处走动。萨莉小姐三十八九岁，这个年纪的女人，只要自己愿意，于眼于心都还未必不惹人喜欢。可她那毫不通融的进言风格，比起她的装束和外表，又算不得什么了。人人裙长曳地时，她穿短裙，好行动自如。人人戴软帽时，她戴一顶系带小帽。她头发稀薄，却恪守本分，绝不添一绪假发，连发垫也不垫一块。她算不上难看，五官端正，眼睛里满是聪慧；至于面色，谈不上有，身段也无可称道。从两人见面那一刻起，她便对米勒弗勒担起了全部灵魂监护之责，而他但凡躲得开，绝不在她身边多待一刻。这逗得全家乐不可支，起初几乎比莉莉还逗。可渐渐地，笑变得勉强，慌乱接替了欢笑。最后还是萨莉·菲尔德小姐本人抓住了牛角——倘若这个比喻不算太亵渎的话。一个晴朗的傍晚，晚饭后众人踱上草坪，她把公爵拉到一旁。「您的儿子，」她说，「正缠着要我嫁他。」她那双聪慧的眼睛直直望着公爵。可以想见，公爵大人懵了。他慨然打量着这个带着大西洋彼岸腔调和神气的中年女人。他不愿失礼。「您！」他狼狈地说，随即为自己的失态红了脸，温文地补了一句：「请您千般见谅——您的意思是——您的侄女。」单是那样就已经够糟了。「不，」萨莉小姐带着遗憾的神气说，「跟莉莉不相干。我同他说过，那样更合情理。莉莉很漂亮，有一大笔钱；可他好像看不见。您或许不知道，当年我打发他回家见母亲，为的就是这个？我原以为他回到家也就想开了。依我看，他完全配不上我；不过那些道德后果，我心里有点不踏实。我三十八岁，有一份中等的进项，不像莉莉那样有财产。我想，这事再往前走之前，还是先同您谈一谈的好。」萨莉小姐说。

And when he took this middle-aged and plainspoken bride to Dalrulzian to visit the young people there, Millefleurs did not attempt to conceal his consciousness of the objections which his friends would no doubt make. “I told you it was quite unsuitable,” he said, turning up his little eyes and clasping his plump hands. “We were both perfectly aware of that; but it is chic, don’t you know, if you will allow me to use a vulgar word.” Edith clasped the arm of John when the Marquis and Marchioness of Millefleurs had retired, and these two young people indulged in subdued bursts of laughter. They stepped out upon the terrace walk to laugh, that they might not be heard, feeling the delightful contrast of their own well-assorted youth and illimitable happiness. The most delightful vanity mingled with their mirth﻿—that vanity in each other which feels like a virtue. It was summer, and the air was soft, the moon shining full over the far sweep of the undulating country, blending with a silvery remnant of daylight which lingered far into the night. The hills in the far distance shone against the lightness of the horizon, and the crest of fir-trees on Dalrulzian hill stood out against the sky, every twig distinct. It was such a night as the lovers babbled of on that bank on which the moonbeams lay at Belmont, but more spiritual than any Italian night because of that soft heavenly lingering of the day which belongs to the north. This young pair had not been married very long, and had not ceased to think their happiness the chief and most reasonable subject of interest to all around them. They were still comparing themselves with everything in earth, and almost in heaven, to the advantage of their own blessedness. They were amused beyond description by the noble couple who had come to visit them. “Confess, now, that you feel a pang of regret,” John said﻿—and they stood closer and closer together, and laughed under their breath as at the most delightful joke in the world. Upstairs the Marchioness shut the window, remarking that the air was very cold. “What a fool that little thing was not to have you,” she said; “you would have done very well together.” “Dear Edith!” said Millefleurs, folding his hands, “it is very pretty, don’t you know, to see her so happy.”

待他带着这位直言无讳的中年新娘回达尔鲁尔齐恩探望那对年轻人时，米勒弗勒也并不掩饰心里明白：朋友们必定大有非议。「我早说过这完全不合适，」他说，翻起他那双小眼睛，合起胖手。「我们两个对这一点都心知肚明；可是这很别致（chic），您明白么——恕我用一个俗词。」米勒弗勒侯爵夫妇退下之后，伊迪丝挕住约翰的手臂，两个年轻人憋着一阵阵低低的笑。他们踱到露台上笑，免得让人听见，满心体味着自家青春匹配、幸福无边的那份美妙反差。最甜的虚荣掺在笑意里——那是对彼此的虚荣，感觉上竟像一种美德。正是夏天，夜气温柔，满月照着远处起伏绵延的旷野，与一缕银白的日光辉光交融——那日光流连不去，直入深夜。极远的群山衬着明亮的天际发亮，达尔鲁尔齐恩山上的杉树冠映在天幕上，枝枝分明。这样的夜晚，正像贝尔蒙特的情人们在月光铺照的河岸上絮语的那种夜晚，却比任何意大利之夜更空灵，因为北方才有这种白昼的柔美天光、徘徊入夜。这对年轻人结婚不久，还不曾停止认为：他们的幸福，是四周所有人首要的、最合情理的关切。他们还在拿自己同人间的万物相比、几乎也同天上的相比，比来比去总归自家的福气占先。来看望他们的这对贵人夫妇，把他们逗得不亦乐乎。「招了吧，你心里可有一丝悔意？」约翰说——两人越站越近，屏着气笑，仿佛天下最妙的笑话。楼上，侯爵夫人关了窗，说夜气很凉。「那小东西真傻，竟没要你，」她说；「你们俩本会很般配的。」「亲爱的伊迪丝！」米勒弗勒合起双手说，「看她这样幸福，多好，您明白么。」

The observations made downstairs, upon the actors in this little drama, were very free, as was natural. Rolls himself, who had held a more important role than anyone knew, was perhaps apt to exaggerate the greatness of his own part, but with an amiable and benevolent effect. His master, indeed, he looked upon with benevolent indulgence, as knowing no more than a child of the chief incident. If Rolls had not been already bound to the house of Dalrulzian by lifelong fidelity and by that identification of himself and all his interests, his pride and self-regard, with his “family,” which is something even more tenacious and real than faithfulness, he would have been made so by the fact that John, without in the slightest degree realising that Rolls was suffering for him, had given orders to Mr. Monypenny to secure the most expensive assistance for his trial. The pride, contempt, satire, and keen suppressed emotion with which this act filled the old servant’s bosom, were beyond description. “It was just downright extravagance,” he said to Bauby; “they’re a’ fuils, thae Erskines, frae father to son. Laying out all that siller upon me; and no’ a glimmer o’ insight a’ the time. An’ he had had the sense to see, it would have been natural; but how could he divine my meaning when there was no conscience in himsel’? and giving out his money all the same as if notes were things ye could gather on the roadside?” “He mightna understand ye, Tammas, but he ken’t your meaning was good,” said Bauby. Their position was changed by all the changes that had happened, to the increase of their grandeur if not of their happiness. Rolls had now a tall and respectful youth under his orders, and Bauby was relieved, in so far as she would allow herself to be relieved, of the duties of the kitchen. It was gratifying to their pride, but there is little doubt that they sighed occasionally for the freedom of the time when Rolls was alone in his glory, dictator of the feminine household, and Bauby’s highest effort of toilette was to tie a clean apron round her ample waist. She had to wear a silk gown now, and endeavour to be happy in it. Rolls’s importance, however, was now publicly acknowledged both out of doors and in.

楼下对这出小戏诸演员的评骘，自然是很放得开的。罗尔斯本人，那个担当了比任何人所知都更重的角色的人，也许容易把自己的戏份夸大几分，效果却和善而仁厚。对主人，他实在是以仁厚的宽容相看，把约翰当作一个对头号大事不比孩子知道得更多的小儿。倘说罗尔斯此前还不曾被终生的忠心、不曾被他与「他的一家人」——他自身的利益、他的骄傲与自尊全同这一家融为一体，比忠心更韧更实的东西——捆在达尔鲁尔齐恩门下，那么这桩事也把他捆牢了：约翰全然没有意识到罗尔斯在替他受难，却吩咐莫尼彭尼先生，为他的庭审请最贵的帮手。这一举在老仆胸中填满的骄傲、鄙夷、讥诣和压抑的激烈情绪，非言语所能形容。「纯粹是挥霍，」他对鲍比说；「厄斯金家的人全是傻子，代代如此。把那么多银子花在我身上；从头到尾没一丝一毫的省悟。他若是有眼看出来，那倒自然；可他自家心里没那杆秤，怎么猜得透我的意思？钱照撒不误，倒像钞票是路边捡得着的物件？」「他兴许不懂你，塔玛斯，可他知道你是好意。」鲍比说。人事种种变迁，也改了两人的位置，气派有增，若说幸福则未必。罗尔斯如今手下有个高个子的恭谨青年听差，鲍比也卸了厨房的差事——在她肯让自己卸下的限度内。这于他们的体面是受用的，可毫无疑问，两人偶尔也要叹想从前那份自在：那时罗尔斯一人独尊，是这女人天地的独裁者，而鲍比妆扮的最高功夫，不过是在她宽大的腰间系一条干净围裙。如今她得穿绸衫，还得努力穿出欢喜来。不过，罗尔斯的分量，如今里里外外都得了公众的承认。

He was looked upon with a kind of admiring awe by the population generally, as a man who had been, as it were, like Dante, in hell, and came out unsinged﻿—or in prison, which was nearly as bad, issuing forth in a sort of halo of innocence and suffering. It might have been possible that John Erskine or any of the gentlemen of the countryside had quarrelled with Tinto and meant mischief; but Rolls could not have meant anything. The very moment that the eyes of the rural world were directed to him, it was established that accident only could be the cause of death, and everybody felt it necessary to testify their sympathy to the unwilling instrument of such an event. The greatest people in the county would stop to speak to him when occasion offered, to show him that they thought no worse of him. Even Lord Lindores would do this; but there was one exception. Rintoul was the one man who had never offered any sympathy. He turned his head the other way when Rolls approached him﻿—would not look at him when they were, perforce, brought into contact. While Rolls, for his part, regarded Lord Rintoul with a cool and cynical air of observation that was infinitely galling to the object of it. “Yon lord!” he said, when he spoke of him, contemptuous, with a scoff always in his tone. And Rolls had grown to be a great authority in legal matters, the only person in the neighbourhood, as was supposed, that knew the mysteries of judicial procedure. But his elevation, as we have said, was modified by domestic drawbacks. Instead of giving forth his sentiments in native freedom as he went and came with the dishes, direct from one table to another, it was necessary to wait until the other servants of the household were disposed of before the butler and the housekeeper could express confidentially their feelings to each other. And Bauby, seated in her silk gown, doing the honours to the Marquis’s man, of whom she stood in great awe, and the Marchioness’s woman, whom she thought a “cutty,” was not half so happy as Bauby, glowing and proud in the praises of a successful dinner, with her clean white apron folded over her arms.

“This is the lord that my leddy would have been married upon, had all gone as was intended,” Rolls said. “He’s my Lord Marquis at present, and will be my Lord Duke in time.”

一般民众看他，带着一种钦佩的敬畏，仿佛一个曾像但丁那样下过地狱、出来时毫发无伤的人——或者蹲过监狱，那也差不多糟——周身罩着一圈清白与受难的光环。约翰·厄斯金或乡下哪位绅士同廷托口角、动了歹念，那还有可能；罗尔斯却不可能存任何歹念。乡野的目光一落到他身上，便已断定死亡只可能是意外，人人都觉得有必要向这桩事的不情愿的工具致一致敬意。郡里顶顶体面的人物，遇到机会总会停下来同他说句话，表示他们不曾看轻他。连林多雷斯勋爵也肯这样做；唯独一个例外。林图尔是唯一从未表示过半分同情的人。罗尔斯走近时，他把头扭向另一边——两人迫不得已碰在一起时，他不肯看他一眼。而罗尔斯那一面，看林图尔勋爵的眼神却是一副冷冷的、玩世的观察，叫被观察的那位窝火到无以复加。「那位老爷！」提起他时他这样说，满是轻蔑，腔调里永远带着一声嗤笑。罗尔斯还成了法律事务上的一位大权威，据说是左近唯一懂得司法程序之奥妙的人。可是如前所说，他的升格受了家内掣肘的折损。再不能像从前那样端着菜来来去去、从这张桌到那张桌、想发什么议论就自由自在地发了；总得等家里其余仆役安顿下去，管家和管家娘子才能彼此说几句体己话。鲍比穿着绸衫坐着，给侯爵的男仆——她畏他如虎——和侯爵夫人的贴身女仆——她认作一个「小蹄子」——张罗应酬，那份快活，不及从前的鲍比一半：围裙干干净净搭在臂弯、在一席成功晚宴的赞美声里红光满面、得意洋洋。

「这就是那位老爷，当年若一切照盘算走，咱们夫人本来要嫁的。」罗尔斯说。「他眼下是侯爵大人，日后就是公爵大人。」

“Such a bit creature for a’ thae grand titles,” said Bauby, yawning freely over the stocking which she was supposed to be knitting. “Eh, Tammas, my man, do ye hear that clatter? We’ll no’ have an ashet left in the house.”

“It’s a peety she didna take him﻿—it would have pleased a’ pairties,” said Rolls. “I had other views mysel’, as is well known, for our maister here, poor lad. Woman, cannot ye bide still when a person is speaking to ye? The ashets are no’ your concern.”

“Eh, and wha’s concern should they be?” cried Bauby; “would I let the family suffer and me sit still? My lady’s just a sweet young thing, and I’m more fond of her every day. She may not just be very clever about ordering the dinner, but what does that maitter as lang as I’m to the fore? And she’s an awfu’ comfort to my mind in respect to Mr. John. It takes off the responsibility. Me that was always thinking what would I say to his mammaw!”

“I have nothing to say against my lady,” said Rolls, “but just that I had ither views. It’s a credit to the house that she should have refused a grand match for *our* sake. But it will be a fine ploy for an observer like me that kens human nature to see them a’ about my table at their dinner the morn. There will be the Earl himsel’, just girning with spite and politeness﻿—and her that would have been my ain choice, maybe beginning to see, poor thing, the mistake she’s made. Poor thing! Marriages, in my opinion, is what most shakes your faith in Providence. It’s just the devil that’s at the bottom o’ them, so far as I can see.”

“Hoot, Tammas﻿—it’s true love that’s at the bottom o’ them,” Bauby said.

“Love!” Rolls cried with contempt: and then he added with a grin of malice﻿—“I’m awfu’ entertained to see *yon lord* at our table-end. He will not look the side I’m on. It’s like poison to him to hear my voice. And I take great pains to serve him mysel’,” he said with a chuckle. “I’m just extraordinar attentive to him. There’s no person that I take half as much charge of. I’m thinking his dinner will choke him some day, for he canna bide the sight o’ me.”

“Him that should go upon his knees to ye every day of his life!” cried Bauby indignant.

“We’ll say nothing about that; but I get my diversion out o’ him,” said Rolls grimly, “though he’s a lord, and I’m but a common man!”

「那么大一个头衔，配上那么一小只人。」鲍比说，对着那只名义上在织的袜子放肆地打哈欠。「嗳，塔玛斯，我的哥，听见那磕碰声没有？家里的盘子（ashet）怕是要一件不剩了。」

「可惜她没要他——那本是皆大欢喜的事。」罗尔斯说。「我自己原另有盘算，这是人人知道的，为的是咱们这位主人，可怜的人。婆娘，人家说话你就不能安坐一会儿？盘子不归你管。」

「嗳，不归我管归谁管？」鲍比喊道；「总不成叫这家人受损失、我干坐着？咱们夫人是个顶甜的年轻人，我一天比一天疼她。安排晚饭这门学问，她兴许不十分在行，可只要我还在，那算得了什么？再说有她在，我这心里对约翰老爷那一头真是天大的安慰。卸了担子了。我从前老想着，回头怎么向他妈妈交代！」

「咱们夫人，我说她一句坏话没有，」罗尔斯说，「只是我原有别的盘算。她肯为了咱们回掉一门天大的亲事，这是这户人家的体面。不过明天，瞧他们一齐围着我的桌子吃晚饭，在我这样一位识得人性的旁观者看来，可是一场好戏。伯爵本人会到场——怨恨和客气一齐蒠着牙——还有那位本会中我意的人儿，可怜的东西，兴许正开始看出自己铸的错。可怜的东西！依我的见识，天下最能叫人不敢再信天意的，就是婚姻。照我看，这底下的根由纯粹是魔鬼。」

「嗐，塔玛斯——这底下的根由是真爱情。」鲍比说。

「爱情！」罗尔斯鄙夷地喊：随即又添上一脸恶意的笑——「看那位老爷坐在我这一端的上首，我可乐坏了。他不肯朝我这一边看。听见我的嗓音，跟灌他毒药似的。可我偏亲自伺候他，费足了心思，」他嘿嘿一笑。「我对他那个殷勤哟。我伺候谁也没这么上心的一半。我看他的晚饭早晚要噎着他，因为他见不得我这个人。」

「他这个人，本该天天给你下跪才是！」鲍比憤憤喊道。

「这且不提；反正我在他身上寻到了消遣，」罗尔斯阴狠地说，「别看他是个老爷，我不过是个平头百姓！」

===Original===

The marriage of Lady Car took place a little more than a year after Torrance’s death. It was accomplished in London, whither she had gone some time before, with scarcely anyone to witness the ceremony but her mother. She preferred it so. She was happy and she was miserable, with the strangest mingling of emotions. Lady Lindores made vain efforts to penetrate into the mind which was no longer open to her as her own. Carry had gone far away from her mother, who knew none of the passions which had swept her soul, yet could divine that the love in which she was so absorbed, the postponed and interrupted happiness which seemed at last to be within her grasp, was not like the love and happiness that might have been. When Beaufort was not with her, her pale countenance, that thoughtful face with its air of *distinction*, and sensitive delicacy, which had never been beautiful, would fall into a wan shadow and fixedness which were wonderful to see. When he was with her, it lighted up with gleams of ineffable feeling, yet would waver and change like a stormy sky, sometimes with a lightning-flash of impatience, sometimes with a wistful questioning glance, which gave it to Lady Lindores all the interest of a poem united to the far deeper, trembling interest of observation with which a mother watches her child on the brink of new possibilities. Were they for good or evil?﻿—was it a life of hope fulfilled, or of ever increasing and deepening disappointment, which lay before Carry’s tremulous feet? They were not the assured feet of a believing and confident bride. What is love without faith and confidence and trust? It is the strangest, the saddest, the most terrible, the most divine of human passions. It is seldom that a woman begins with such enlightenment in her eyes. Usually it is the growth of slow and much-resisted experience, the growing revelation of years. How sweet, how heavenly, how delightful, when love is blind! How wise the ancients were to make him a child﻿—a thing of caprice and sweet confusion, taking everything for granted! But this to Carry was impossible. When her mother took her into her arms on her wedding morning, dressed in the soft grey gown which was the substitute for bridal white, they kissed each other with a certain solemnity. At such a moment so much is divined between kindred hearts which words can never say.

===Chinese===

卡丽夫人的婚礼，在托伦斯死后一年多一点的时候举行。是在伦敦办的她早些时日就去了那里，观礼的除她母亲之外几乎没有旁人。她宁肯这样。她幸福，她又悲苦，种种情绪纠缠得再奇怪不过。林多雷斯夫人想探进那颗心，却徒劳无功——它已不再像她自己的一样向她敞开。卡丽离母亲远了，那些席卷过她灵魂的种种激情，母亲一样也不识，却猜得出：她沉溺其中的那份爱，那份似乎终于到手了的、被延误、被打断过的幸福，不同于本来可能有的爱与幸福。博福特不在跟前时，她那张苍白的脸——那张若有所思的脸，带着名门气韵与敏感的细腻，从来算不上美——会沉入一种惨淡的阴翳与凝定，看着叫人心惊。博福特在跟前时，它便亮起难以言传的感情的光，却又像多变的天色摇晃变换，时而一道不耐烦的闪电，时而一瞥怅然的疑问，使它在林多雷斯夫人眼里，兼有一首诗的全部兴味，和一种深得多、颤得多的观察的兴味——一位母亲望着自己孩子站在新机遇的边缘上时的那种观察。那机遇是福是祸？——铺在卡丽颤巍巍脚下等着的，是希望成真的一生，还是日益加深、愈积愈重的失望的一生？那不是笃信而自信的新娘那双踏实的脚。没有信仰、没有把握、没有信托的爱是什么？它是人类激情里最奇异、最悲哀、最可怕、也最神圣的一种。一个女人起头眼里就带着这般彻悟，是少有的事。那照例是缓慢而极力抗拒的经验养出来的，是岁月一层层揭开启示。爱是盲目的时候，多么甜蜜，多么如登天国，多么欢畅！古人多么智慧，把爱神做成一个孩子——一件任性而甜蜜昏乱的物事，把一切想当然！可这一层于卡丽是不可能的。婚礼的早晨，母亲把她搂进怀里——她穿着一袭柔软的灰裙，那便是新娘白的替身——两人带着几分庄严彼此相吻。这样的时刻，两颗血亲的心之间所默契的，远非言语所能说尽。

===Original===

“I want you to remember,” said Carry, “mother dear﻿—that whatever comes of it, this is what is best.” “I hope all that is most happy will come of it, my darling,” said Lady Lindores. “And I too﻿—and I too﻿—” She paused, raising a little her slender throat, her face, that was like a wistful pale sky, clear-shining after the rain﻿—“But let it be what it may, it is the only good﻿—the only way for me.” These were the sole words explanatory that passed between them. Lady Lindores parted with the bridal pair afterwards with an anxious heart. She went home that night, travelling far in the dark through the unseen country, feeling the unknown all about her. Life had not been perfect to her any more than to others. She had known many disappointments, and seen through many illusions: but she had preserved through all the sweetness of a heart that can be deceived, that can forget today’s griefs and hope again in tomorrow as if today had never been. As she drew near her home, her heart lightened without any reason at all. Her husband was not a perfect mate for her﻿—her son had failed to her hopes. But she did not dwell on these disenchantments. After all, how dear they were! after all, there was tomorrow to come, which perhaps, most likely, would yet be the perfect day.

===Chinese===

「我要你记住，」卡丽说，「亲爱的妈妈——无论后来生出什么，这一步是最好的。」「我盼着后来生出的是最大的幸福，我的宝贝。」林多雷斯夫人说。「我也盼——我也盼——」她顿了顿，纤细的脖颈微微扬起，她的脸像一片怅然的、雨后初霁的淡色天空——「可无论它是什么，它是唯一的善——我唯一的路。」两人之间说破的话，就只有这几句。随后，林多雷斯夫人怀着忐忑的心送走了这对新人。当夜她踏上归途，在黑暗里穿行很远的路，走过看不见的田野，只觉未知四面围拢。生命于她，也同旁人一样不曾完满。她经历过许多失望，看穿过许多幻象：可她自始至终保有一颗心的甜——一颗还会受骗的心，一颗能忘掉今天的悲伤、又在明天重新指望的心，仿佛今天从来不曾有过。将近家门时，她的心没来由地轻快起来。她的丈夫于她并非完美的伴侣——她的儿子负了她的指望。可她不在这几重幻灭上逗留。到底，他们多么亲啊！到底，明天还会来，而明天，多半、多半就是那个圆满的日子。

===Original===

“Two of the sweet’st companions in the world.”

> *Cymbeline*

===Chinese===

「世上再甜蜜不过的一对侣伴。」

> 《辛白林》
